C. Anderson Wat the Tinker/Guy of Gisbourne/Richard Partington/Quince the Cobbler/Director of the Sport/Judge/Blacksmith: Gerald Moe King Richard/Old Friar: Weretortoise The Lord Bishop of Hereford/Lean Brother Ambrose/Forester 1/William of the Scar/Gilbert o' the Red Cap: Beeswaxcandle Will Stutely: rickwhitaker King Henry the Second/Midge, the Miller's son: Justin Clevenger Allen a Dale: HelloCentral Cook/The Corn Engrosser/Prior Vincent/Sir Robert Lee/Beggar/Sir Hubert of Gingham/Edward of Deirwold/Sir Amyas o' the Dell: AffableAmateur Queen Eleanor/Maken of the Blue Boar/Peddler/Forester 3/The "Dumb" Beggar/Lass 1: ShrimpPhish David of Doncaster/The Butcher/The "Blind" Beggar/Forester 4: Douglas Allen Minor role(s) performed by: Glys , mleigh , Belinda Mc , Greg Giordano , Jenn Broda , JenNoel , David Purdy , Levi Justus , Eowyn Bree

22495.d: When Josiah Crowley died, no one expected his entire fortune to go to the greedy and unpopular Tophams. Nancy Drew is convinced that there is another will somewhere. And where there is a will, there's a way... - Summary by ShrimpPhish

22496.d: This is the 19th Librivox Short Mystery and Suspense Collection. Readers select their own stories to read, of less than about 60 minutes duration. Please ask if you are unsure of copyright status. - Summary by LynneT

22497.d: Stories of might and main, romance and tragedy among the Tuatha DeDanaan with Brigit, Lir, Manannaun, Ethaun and others. Great ancient gods of wind, water and earth and their children mingle with people of the Faeries, heroes and the after-world. Told with poetry and wit by Ella Young in an old and familiar 'honey-sweet wisdom of speech'. An important part of the Celtic revival in Ireland.- Summary by Czandra

22498.d: Poetry, fairy world of Ireland - Summary by Czandra

22499.d: Le célèbre détective Sherlock Holmes et son acolyte, Docteur John Watson apportent leur aide à Miss Mary Morstan afin de résoudre une nouvelle affaire. Cette dernière fait appel à eux afin qu'ils enquêtent sur la disparition troublante de son père qui les mènera au cœur d'une intrigue mystérieuse impliquant un trésor. - Summary by MaryMédia
22499.tr: Jeanne de Polignac, Comtesse d' Oilliamson

22500.d: In the years following World War I, immigration was a hot topic in the United States. The number of immigrants arriving each year had surged, and many came from East Asian or Southern European cultures that seemed alien to Americans of Northern European descent. Political parties began drafting legislation to further restrict immigration. Yet opposition to immigration was not universal; many people continued to support more open borders. This issue—and some of the arguments on both sides—will sound familiar to readers today, almost anywhere in the world. One notable difference, however, lies in the media through which the debate was conducted. Today, discussions unfold largely through podcasts, television news, and social media. In the early twentieth century, by contrast, people relied almost entirely on print for mass communication, informing themselves through major newspapers and national magazines. This concise 1920 book summarizes the debate over immigration restriction and presents reprints of articles offering a range of arguments and analyses. - Summary by Ted Lienhart

22501.d: A biographical account of the life of Founding Father John Jay, who was a co-author of The Federalist Papers and served in various positions in government such as Governor of New York, a member of the Continental Congress, and the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. John Jay was an early abolitionist, a signer of the Continental Association and author of the Jay Treaty which permanently established the United States through peace with Great Britain. Included are papers and correspondence of John Jay. - Summary by progressingamerica

22502.d: Count Felix von Luckner, German naval war officer of World War One, through the words of Lowell Thomas, relates his adventures at sea as a young man through his German naval command in Word War I. Von Luckner is best known as the one who broke through the British blockade and disrupted Allied shipping in a windjammer, under sail, while managing to avoid killing any Allied crews. (Summary by Mark Harrington)

22503.d: Michael Trahearne, searching out his supposed Breton ancestry, is astonished to learn that he is a member of the galaxy’s only race capable of interstellar travel, the Vardda. He is even more astonished, over and over (as the reader will be) as his immersion in his new culture entangles him in trade, love, hatred, treachery, conspiracy, and the rival efforts to find out or keep hidden his new culture’s most prized but deepest, darkest, most dangerous secret. "The Starmen of Llyrdis" (Startling Stories, March 1951) Copyright not renewed. - Summary by Mokurai

22504.d: A love story of Charudatta and Vasantasena navigating social class, political intrigue, and jealousy. - Summary by dc

22505.d: The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, was written by King David and various other authors over a period of several hundred years beginning around 1000 BC. It consists of divinely inspired hymn-like poems expressing the heart of lives lived in God's presence. Myles Coverdale's translation was used in the Book of Common Prayer from 1662-1979 and is currently used in the Divine Worship Daily Office of the (Roman Catholic) Ordinariate of the Chair of Saint Peter. This edition of the Psalms is divided into daily readings for Morning and Evening Prayer which cover the Psalter in a month. - Summary by Russell Hobbs

22506.d: Collection of 3 short stories drawn from the author's childhood experiences of mingling with Romanies. - Summary by LynneT

22507.d: A tale of high adventure and international intrigue.... Maurice Wynn, the investigative journalist, finds himself involved in the mysterious murder of the man upstairs. In an attempt to protect the woman he loves, he embarks on an adventure bigger than he ever imagined. (Summary by MamaPhish and ShrimpPhish)

22508.d: Genesis, the beginning of the Holy Bible, the beginning of God's creation & of His people; "seed plot of the Bible". Gleanings in Genesis is a distinctive devotional-theological reading of Genesis. Moving sequentially through Genesis, Pink goes beyond the surface narrative to reveal patterns, symbols, and doctrinal seeds that, in his view, foreshadow the arrival of Christ & His message of redemption & salvation. Thus, Pink presents Genesis, not as a mere historical record of the beginning, but a blueprint of Christianity flowing throughout the Scripture up till the end, The Revelations. This book gives a theological & spiritual perspective of the Book of Genesis. - Summary by sonaliie

22509.d: Ramey Winters and his fellow airman Red Barrett meet up with Archeologists in Cambodia during WWII, just before the Indo-China involvement in the conflict. Their adventures span centuries and bring a new understanding to old mysteries. Honor, sacrifice, time-travel and the pitfalls of colonization are all explored in this wonderfully written mystery adventure! (Summary by Cindy Morton)

22510.d: Political history figured large in volume 110 of the Short Nonfiction Collection, with reader chosen topics ranging from the Scottish Declaration of Arboarth (1320), to the battle of Cape St. Vincent (1797), early exploration of the North Pacific ocean, Thomas Jefferson's last testament, and Abraham Lincoln's character and legacy. Other readers chose scientific topics: repeating cycles in British climate, ink blot personality testing, animal suicide, cholera transmission, and theories about sleep. Summary by Sue Anderson

22511.d: The Black Cat (1895-1922) was a monthly literary magazine, publishing original short stories, often about uncanny or fantastical topics. Many writers were largely unknown, but some famous authors also wrote original material for this magazine. Volume 6 Number 5 has the following stories: > The Smile of Joss, by William J. Neidig: sometimes one has to pray at a different altar in order to survive > The Sins of Sims, by Harle Oren Cummins: a bellboy is sent on the most exciting errand of his career > The Unassimilated Miss Downing, by Edward Stratton Holloway: a young lady gets entangled in a spy plot > The Cross on the Plain, by George Dyre Eldridge: witness a man's struggle to escape from the deadly plain > The Rhyme for Rachel, by Clifford Howard: will a rhyme be found for this lady's name ? - Summary by Sonia

22512.d: In September 1941, Colonel Samuel L. Howard, USMC, Commanding Officer, 4th Marines, recommended to Admiral Thomas Hart, USN, Commander-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, that Howard's regiment be evacuated from its longtime duty station in Shanghai. The regiment comprised two small battalions, made up of approximately 800 Marines and attached naval personnel, and was dangerously exposed to Japanese attack should war come. On 10 November 1941, Colonel Howard received the long-awaited orders to prepare the withdrawal of his regiment [to the Philippines]. On 3 December, Colonel Howard reported to Admiral Hart in Manila to discuss the mission of the regiment. The 4th Marines was put under the command of Rear Admiral Francis W. Rockwell, commanding the 16th Naval District, and given the mission of protecting the naval stations on the island of Luzon, primarily Olongapo and the Navy Section Base at Mariveles. The Comman-der-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, stressed a more important mission to Howard. That mission was to prepare his men for mobile field operations. Hart also underscored the proximity to war with the Japanese. - Summary by J. Michael Miller

22513.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 17 recordings of Ebb and Flow by George William Curtis. This was the Weekly Poetry project for April 5, 2026. ------ George William Curtis was an American writer, reformer, public speaker, and political activist. In 1862 George William Curtis delivered his "Doctrine of Liberty" address to Phi Beta Kappa society at Harvard, on behalf of President Abraham Lincoln, who was encouraging support for the Emancipation Proclamation. In it, he laid out the intellectual foundations for the purpose of American education that would last another 30 years, and public schools, nearly 100 years. - Summary by Wikipedia

22514.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 10 recordings of April Morning by Evaleen Stein. This was the Fortnightly Poetry project for April 5, 2026. ------ Evaleen Stein was an American writer and poet as well as a limner. She was the author of eleven volumes of stories and three books of verse. In addition, she translated two volumes of poetry, one from the Japanese (When Fairies Were Friendly) and another from Italian. - Summary by Wikipedia

22515.d: In the shadow-drenched halls of Collingwood Estate, Mary Jane Holmes explores the delicate intersection of tragedy and redemption. Darkness and Daylight introduces us to Edith Hastings, a girl of unknown lineage, and Richard Harrington, a man whose physical blindness is matched only by his internal grief. As Edith grows from a rescued waif into a woman of character, her world expands to include the volatile Nina and the watchful Arthur St. Claire. It is a story where secrets are the currency, and the ultimate climax hinges on a single question: can love ever truly outweigh the weight of a lifelong debt? - Summary by Celine Major

22516.d: Science fiction is a genre encompassing imaginative works that take place in this world or that of the author’s creation where anything is possible. The only rules are those set forth by the author. The speculative nature of the genre inspires thought and plants seeds that have led to advances in science. The genre can spark an interest in the sciences and is cited as the impetus for the career choice of many scientists. It is a playing field to explore social perspectives, predictions of the future, and engage in adventures unbound into the richness of the human mind. - Summary by A. Gramour

22517.d: This collection of recipes begins with an extended history of Crisco, tips for cooks, methods of cooking, and "The Art of Carving." Recipes are organized by category from Soups to Candies and Vegetarian dishes. Then follows a calendar of dinners for each month from January through December. - Summary by Larry Wilson

22518.d: The National Geographic Magazine, an illustrated monthly, Vol XII, April 1901. It includes the following articles: The Old Yuma Trail (Part 2), by W.J. McGee Advances In Geographic Knowledge During The Nineteenth Century, by Brig. Gen. A.W. Greely Mexico Of Today (Part 1), by Dr. Don Juan N. Navarro Geographic Notes & Literature Proceedings Of The National Geographic Society - Summary by mungojerry311

22519.d: The fates of a war-torn France and an England faded of its past glory hang in the balance in this first installment of William Shakespeare’s riveting Wars of the Roses tetralogy. Following the untimely death of King Henry V, lofty ambitions and heated rivalries come the fore in the English court as various members of the nobility vie for power and favour before the coronation of the late king’s young and callow son. Meanwhile, the new monarch’s ascension to the throne is further complicated by the English army’s territorial losses in France. Despite the valiant efforts of the noble Lord Talbot, who fights fiercely to defend England’s claims, the arrival of the mysterious maiden Joan la Pucelle (who we now know today as Joan of Arc) on the French side signals a drastic tidal shift. Before long, Joan’s determination and passion in battle inspire the French to resist against their invaders, while the simmering tensions and splintered factions back in England weaken the country’s hold in the geopolitical sphere, opening the door for further discord and treachery in the plays to follow. Filled with stirring speeches, vivid characters and memorable battle scenes, this gripping opening chapter of Shakespeare’s original tetralogy invites audiences into a sweeping saga of power, patriotism and the human cost of war. And to perform it all? Three men ( Craig Franklin , Tomas Peter , and Brad “Hamlet” Filippone ) and three women ( Sonia , Jenn Broda , and Kelly S. Taylor ), determined to give you a performance of Shakespeare's work that you will never forget. You thought you knew your Shakespeare? Well, think again! - Summary by Tomas Peter Cast List: Jenn Broda : Narrator; Duke of Gloucester; Duke of Alençon; Sir William Lucy; Countess of Auvergne; Boy; Lawyer; First Gaoler; French Soldier; Servant to Talbot. Sonia : Joan la Pucelle; Bishop/Cardinal of Winchester; Vernon; Earl of Salisbury; Third Serving-man to Gloucester; Second Messenger to the English Court; Second Warder; First French Sentinel; Messenger to the Countess of Auvergne; Messenger to York. Craig Franklin : King Henry VI; Lord Talbot; Bastard of Orleans; Old Shepherd; First Messenger to the English Court; First Warder; Officer to the Mayor of London; Second French Sentinel. Kelly S. Taylor : Charles; Duke of Bedford; Earl/Duke of Somerset; Margaret; First Serving-man to Gloucester; Master-Gunner of Orleans; Messenger to Talbot; French General; Porter; Papal Legate. Tomas Peter : Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York; Reignier; Earl of Warwick; John Talbot; English Captain; Second Serving-man to Gloucester; Woodvile; Sir William Glansdale; Third Messenger to the English Court; French Sergeant; French Watchman; French Scout. Brad “Hamlet” Filippone : Earl of Suffolk; Duke of Burgundy; Duke of Exeter; Mayor of London; Basset; Sir John Fastolfe; Edmund Mortimer; Sir Thomas Gargrave; English Soldier .

22520.d: A collection of short Aesop’s fables presented in English, Chinese, and Spanish. These brief animal stories convey simple moral lessons in a gentle, bedtime-friendly style. - Summary by LydiaX

22521.d: Little Nah-tee has been separated from her family in the American southwest desert! Brave and full of life, she accepts the help of Moyo. They have exciting and wondrous adventures in their quest for her people. Published in 1928, Grace Moon writes of the people she dearly loved and lived with. The word “papoose,” being Algonquin and Narragansett, would not have been used by the Puebloan or Navajo peoples, but this novel is a respectful tale that is a refreshing departure from the racism of Moon’s era. This was a 1929 Newbery Honor Book. - Summary by Lynette Caulkins

22522.d: Household Words was an English weekly magazine edited by Charles Dickens in the 1850s. It took its name from the line in Shakespeare's Henry V: "Familiar in his mouth as household words." The topics ranged widely and included fiction, non-fiction and poetry. - Summary by LynneT

22523.d: Leslie Francis Silberberg's debut sci-fi publication, under the pen name Leslie F. Stone, begins with the story of a New Jersey fishing trip turned alien abduction. The narrator is whisked away to a far world where veganism and gender equality are the norm but unfortunately chattel slavery is still rife. There he learns the story of the individual who arrived before him, one Dana Gleason, who discovered love, purpose, and a new identity on the way to a planet-wide revolution. - Summary by Nicole J. LeBoeuf

22524.d: Today we are bombarded with the idea that forensic science can be used to solve almost any crime. At the turn of the twentieth century, forensic science was in its infancy, but Ainsworth Mitchell was a leader in the field. He was head of investigation at Scotland Yard and was frequently called as an expert witness. His areas of expertise were handwriting analysis and document authentication. His background was in chemistry. - Summary by LynneT

22525.d: A human, touching ghost-story about a lover who returned from the grave to blight his sweetheart’s happiness! - Summary by Weird Tales, June 1927

22527.d: La raccolta delle principali opere in versi di Giacomo Leopardi. Il testo di riferimento è una storica edizione scolastica e di commento dei Canti leopardiani, pubblicata dalla casa editrice G.C. Sansoni di Firenze nel 1919, basata su di una prima edizione del 1892. Comprende sostanzialmente i canti dell'edizione napoletana dell'editore Saverio Starita che Leopardi stesso curò nel 1835, e le aggiunte successive introdotte principalmente a cura dell’amico Antonio Ranieri, incluse “Il tramonto della luna” e “La ginestra” (composte a Torre del Greco nel 1836), e inoltre l’aggiunta del Coro di Morti nello studio di Federico Ruysch” tratto dall'operetta morale Dialogo di Federico Ruysche delle Mummie. (Riassunto di Pier)

22528.d: He knew perfectly well that it was almost impossible to operate on those low wave-lengths with the apparatus in existence at that time—hence his sardonic proposal. The amateurs, however, refused to “die out.” Faced with the inexorable regulation, they set to work to devise apparatus which would operate successfully. Among them was E. H. Armstrong, a youth who at that time was attending Columbia. - Summary by Jack Binns

22529.d: This work is a peculiar discussion of the philosophy of clothing, purported to be based on a work by a mysterious German professor of "Things in General" whose life and times are extensively discussed as well as aspects of his philosophy. The novel reaches deep into many philosophical and anthropological considerations. It is written with a large infusion of irony and Carlyle's typical panache. (Summary by Peter Tucker)

22530.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 15 recordings of April by Richard Le Gallienne. This was the Weekly Poetry project for April 12, 2026. ------ Richard Le Gallienne was an English author and poet. Our tribute to Spring this week is taken from The Lonely Dancer and Other Poems (1913) - Summary by David Lawrence

22531.d: Dr. Stalker's essays on the Seven Deadly Sins contain many timely hints for conduct, and touch some delicate subjects with much sagacity. The order followed is that indicated by the scholastic mnemonic Saligia, which is made up of the initial letters of Superbia, Avaritia, Luxuria, Invidia, Gula, Ira, Accidia. The subject is somewhat of a novelty in Protestant religious literature, and it is handled in a way that should provoke thought. - Summary by The London Quarterly and Holborn Review

22532.d: This is the fifth book in the New Testament, the Book of Acts. It is a history of the early church. - Summary by Julie Anne Thompson

22533.d: Semple outlines how the development of civilisation across the American continent has been shaped the extensive variety of geographic and environmental conditions, which continue to shape history through patterns of economic growth. - Summary by Leon Harvey

22534.d: Its Votaries and Victims, in All Times and Countries, Especially in England and in France. NOTE: As with all historical texts, the language used in this volume should be interpreted within the context of the entire work and the cultural context of its publication. - Summary by Subtitle

22535.d: Mother Earth, an American anarchist journal, was self styled as "A Monthly Magazine Devoted to Social Science and Literature". Mother Earth was initiated in 1906. Its first editor was Emma Goldman, an activist in the United States. Contemporary activists and writers in Europe as well as the US contributed to its pages. In addition, it contained essays by historic figures. This is Volume 1 of the series. - Summary by Christine Rottger

22536.d: Book 9 of the Adventure Stories for Girls Series. Florence and Betty travel to France with their friend Madam Strosser. While visiting the forests and small villages in a simple wagon, they stumble upon an American soldier who had been wounded in the war ten years ago, and who was looking for a dugout that held a treasure. The treasure had been stolen by the Germans from a small town for whom it was their only source of tourist income. While on this quest, they also come across several gypsies and a young blond-haired lady who seems to be mysteriously connected with them. Travel with these young ladies as they see many of the wonders of France, and use their courage and creativity to succeed. (Summary by Keith Salis)

22537.d: For a late Victorian Briton, to be "in chancery" could mean literally to be involved in a law suit (such as, for example, a divorce suit) being heard in a Court of Chancery, or, more broadly, to be trapped in any awkward predicament almost impossible to untangle (as law suits heard in the Court of Chancery often tended to be). In this, the second volume of The Forsyte Saga, wealthy lawyer Soames Forsyte struggles to free himself from a situation he finds almost impossibly awkward, given the divorce laws of his time. Though it is now a dozen or so years since he and his wife Irene split up, they have never divorced. Soames is now desperate to have a son. What can he do? He knows that Irene is now keeping company with his cousin Jolyon. Can he persuade her to come back to him? Or should he, instead, take the risky course of attempting to prove to the world that the woman he still aches after is an adulteress, publicly shame her and divorce her, and marry a pretty French woman half his age in hopes that she will bear him the son he craves? (Summary by Peter Dann)

22538.d: Die Abenteuer des Tom Sawyer waren gedacht zunächst, so der Autor des Buches Mark Twain in einer Selbsteinschätzung, für ihn selbst vor allem eine Art „Fingerübung“ - für seine Leserinnen und Leser jeden Alters ist der „Tom Sawyer“ aber seit seiner Erstveröffentlichung im Jahr 1876 - übrigens zeitgleich im englischen Original in den USA und in einer ersten Übersetzung ins Deutsche durch den Bismarck-Biografen Moritz Busch, die ich hier lese - einer der unübertroffenen Klassiker der Jugendliteratur. Neben Tom und seinen Freunden Joe Harper und dem Outlaw-Bengel Huckleberry Finn spielen das Mädchen Becky Thatcher, Tochter eines angesehenen Richters im Mississippi-Städtchen Petersburg, wo die Geschichte spielt, die Tante Polly, sein Halbbruder, der Musterknabe Sid, sowie der mörderische Indianer-Joeund der Landstreicher Muff Potter wichtige Rollen; nicht zu vergessen eine Insel im Mississippi, und eine geheimnisvolle Höhle, in der ein Schatz zu einem Happy-End führt. - Summary by Jos van Aken

22539.d: This book brings together accounts of German spies operating in Great Britain during World War I, along with the methods British counter-espionage agents used to track them down. The German Secret Service began building a network of agents in Britain as early as 1905, mainly to gather information about naval operations. By the time war broke out in the summer of 1914, British authorities were already aware of many of these spies and quickly moved to keep them under watch. Britain’s willingness to devote more resources to counterintelligence than Germany put into spying—along with a patient approach to observing enemy activity—played a major role in its success in largely shutting down German espionage efforts. (Summary by Ted Lienhart)

22540.d: Anne of Green Gables is a beloved children's book and a popular text for readers at Librivox. The first version was completed in March of 2006, less than a year after Librivox was founded. Twenty years later, a new set of readers has contributed their voices to this collaborative reading. We hope you enjoy listening as much as we enjoyed reading it! - Summary by MaryAnn

22541.d: A collection of free-standing humorous short stories written by famous as well as more obscure authors: I'm in a Hurry by William Hazlett Upson The Custody of the Pumpkin by P. G. Wodehouse The Milky Way by Stewart Edward White La Bella Gina by Eleanor Mercein Kelly Classics in Slang: Robinson Crusoe by H. C. Witwer The Pusher-In-The-Face by F. Scott Fitzgerald Almost a Gentleman by Edward Hope Arabian Knights by Octavus Roy Cohen The Sixth McNally by Montague Glass Zone of Quiet by Ring W. Lardner (Summary by MamaPhish)

22542.d: A collection of stories that takes you into a magical land which tests courage, loyalty, and the power of hope. The mood shifts between quiet tenderness and eerie stillness, building toward a suspenseful, dreamlike adventure. - Summary by Gerald Moe

22543.d: Blanche Taylor Dickinson was an author and educator from Kentucky. These poems were published between 1927 and 1929. - Summary by Newgatenovelist

22544.d: Dentro del llamado ciclo micénico Eurípides hace una versión muy particular de la historia de Orestes. Datada en el año 408 a.C. esta obra supone la continuación de Electra. Eurípides aborda el mito de una manera radicalmente distinta a como lo hacen los dos grandes tragediógrafos que le preceden –Esquilo y Sófocles. Orestes intenta hacer interceder a su tío Menelao para no ser condenado a muerte junto con su hermana Electra por haber terminado con la vida de su propia madre, Clitemnestra. La negativa de Menelao, por intereses espurios, propicia un desenlace absolutamente inesperado que seguramente ha inspirado muchos de los finales de las tragedias shakespirianas llenas de sangre y amor. El argumento y personajes enlazan con otros tres dramas de Eurípides, siendo éste el tercero, siguiendo el ciclo que empezó con "Ifigenia en Áulide" continua la trama en "Electra", y finaliza con "Ifigenia entre los Tauros" que desarrollan las desventuras de los hijos del rey Agamenón, de la dinastía de los Átridas (Introducción por gabrielledosuarez)

22545.d: Three inseparable girls, school chums that begin boarding school. They learn new sports and make new friends. They work on solving a couple of mysteries that happen at the school. They also deal with the mean girls that are making life difficult for them. A great read for girls of any age. (Summary by NLizer)

22546.d: Household Words was an English weekly magazine edited by Charles Dickens in the 1850s. It took its name from the line in Shakespeare's Henry V: "Familiar in his mouth as household words." The subject matter was varied, including poetry, fiction, non-fiction and opinions. - Summary by LynneT

22547.d: Pastors and Masters (1925) is the first of Ivy Compton-Burnett's 19 published novels. A critic for The New Statesman wrote: "It is astonishing, amazing. It is like nothing else in the world. It is a work of genius." In it, Compton-Burnett introduces her famously acerbic style using only clipped, sharp dialogue. One isn't sure whether it is comic, tragic, or camp (as Susan Sontag averred). It is largely a character study, dealing with themes of literary ambition, intellectual property and plagiarism, tyranny, female subservience, and unconventional sexuality within the setting of an English boys’ preparatory school. - Summary by Rick Whitaker

22548.d: The writings of Justin Martyr are among the most important that have come down to us from the second century. He was not the first that wrote an Apology in behalf of the Christians, but his Apologies are the earliest extant. They are characterized by intense Christian fervour, and they give us an insight into the relations existing between heathens and Christians in those days. His other principal writing, the Dialogue with Trypho, is the first elaborate exposition of the reasons for regarding Christ as the Messiah of the Old Testament, and the first systematic attempt to exhibit the false position of the Jews in regard to Christianity. - Summary by Introductory Notice Justin: Beeswaxcandle Trypho/Old Man/Companion 2 of Trypho/A Pythagorean/Companion 1 of Trypho: InTheDesert

22549.d: Alice is sitting sleepily by the fire-side with the cat, Dinah, and her two kittens. The looking glass on the wall over the fire seems to reflect the room Alice is sitting in, but she wonders whether, out of her sight, the world beyond really is the same as her own. And when the mirror fades away like mist, she climbs through into the looking glass room beyond and finds it very strange; the world beyond her front door appears to be divided into squares "just like a chessboard". A new world to explore! - Summary by Peter Yearsley

22550.d: The first book in the Penny Parker Mystery Series. Written by the author of the Nancy Drew Mystery Series. - Summary by Amanda Leung

22551.d: Fiktiver Roman der auf historischen Tatsachen beruht. Es ist die Geschichte eines Engländers, der zuerst im 30jährigen Krieg unter dem schwedischen König dient, und danach unter Charles I. im englischen Bürgerkrieg. Zusammenfassung von Katharina21

22552.d: Fans of historical true crime will enjoy Great Detectives and Their Methods . Published in 1928, it draws primarily from later 19th-century cases. The majority are Scotland Yard investigations, though Dilnot also includes some American, French, and German cases. The crimes range from scams and con jobs to murders and robberies. Each chapter highlights a different detective, with some particularly interesting case he solved, typically using some ingenious method. - Summary by Verla Viera

22553.d: Four-month-old Mary Craig is the idol and sole heir of her wealthy grandfather. Her parents are dead; her grandfather's other descendants have been disowned or disinherited. He protects her like a priceless treasure to the point of paranoia. And then the unthinkable happens: she is kidnapped. The kidnapper is killed before revealing her whereabouts. On his deathbed, the grandfather updates his will so that if Mary is not found before she is twenty-one, his other grandchild, Henry, should inherit the estate. And Mary? She grows up in a fishing village, not knowing who she is. When she's eighteen, circumstances and her own desires to leave drive her from the only home she's known, yet has never fit into. This book is a novelization of a play and several stories that originally appeared in the Ladies' World magazine in 1913. - Summary by TriciaG

22554.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 15 recordings of Désespoir by Oscar Wilde. This was the Weekly Poetry project for April 19, 2026. ------ "This collection of Wilde’s Poems contains the volume of 1881 in its entirety. Two new poems, ‘Désespoir’ and ‘Pan,’ which I have recently discovered in manuscript, are now printed for the first time." (Robert Ross from the introduction to Poems by Oscar Wilde) - Summary by David Lawrence

22555.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 9 recordings of The Smack in School by William Pitt Palmer. This was the Fortnightly Poetry project for April 19, 2026. ------ This Fortnightly poem is taken from Echoes of half a century; poems, by William Pitt Palmer (1880). William Pitt Palmer was an American poet and hymn writer. While not as widely known as some of his contemporaries, Palmer contributed significantly to American hymnody with his heartfelt and devout compositions.

22556.d: Entertaining Narratives and Anecdotes Illustrative of Principles and Character - Summary by Subtitle

22557.d: Do you love nature? Do you like national parks? Thank George P. Marsh's "Man and Nature", written in 1864, for pioneering the study and the preservation of our environment. By focusing on how humanity's actions affect nature around us, Marsh influenced the discussion of caring for the environment, and the eventual creation of national parks, forests, and refuges. As a result, worldwide, as of 2022, 15% of land, and 8% of sea have been protected for preservation. - Summary by mpinedag

22558.d: After a failed attempt at mutiny, three men are sentenced to be stranded on a wild and dangerous planet in an unfamiliar solar system. Can they survive the viscous flesh-eating plants, the hideous reptilian pygmies, the giant flying bird creatures and even worse monstrosities which imperil them at every turn? - Summary by Ben Tucker

22559.d: This early novel, a collection of biographical tales about a nonfictional individual, a clothier, provides a rare glimpse of daily life in an industry during the early years of King Henry VIII's reign. The author's ingenuous style, occasionally addressing the reader directly in the second person, creates the atmosphere of an informal exchange of tales around a cracker barrel. Many of the tales have explicit morals, for Jack is a businessman with a heart of gold, the very opposite of the unreformed Ebenezer Scrooge. He proves that generosity rather than parsimony is the key to success. An imaginative innovator, he unites the clothiers of England during a national emergency to appeal to the king for redress—and for his pains faces bureaucratic opposition similar to that which, centuries later, was to afflict union leaders. However, as true history most of the book must be taken with a grain or salt, as the amusing preface points out. - Summary by Thomas A. Copeland

22560.d: As I walk’d by myself, And talked to myself, Myself said unto me— Through many changing seasons these tales have walked and talked with me. They were not meant for printing; I have left them in the homely idiom of our old north country speech. I send them on the insistence of friends beyond the sea. BEATRIX POTTER. - Summary by Beatrix Potter

22561.d: The first book in the Matilda series, this book follows Matilda in her life as a Christian. Matilda strives to live a life of religious devotion, service, and moral fortitude while navigating the challenges of growing up, social constraints, and family issues. - Summary by Jessie Percival

22562.d: Mid Century Science Fiction Classic! Dr Gary Lane has made a scientific discovery that there is an active plot against our solar system! Since the plot originates from outside the galaxy, he and his companions must gather resources and assistance from each of the inhabited worlds to be able to travel beyond the systems edge and confront the root of the conspiracy. With an impending time constraint of universal annihilation and a local adversary trying to keep the expedition from happening, mystery and intrigue abound! (Summary by Cindy Morton)

22563.d: A collection of 40 Slavonic Fairy Tales collected and translated from the Russian, Polish, Servian, and Bohemian by John T. Naaké of the British Museum. - Summary by Title page

22564.d: Władysław Umiński, zwany polskim Julesem Verne’em, opowiada historię astronoma Edwina Hartinga, który wybiera się na podróż do Ekwadoru, gdzie stara się wysłać sygnał na Marsa i dowiedzieć się, czy istnieje na nim życie rozumne. Książka była też wydana pod tytułem 'Na Drugą Planetę'. Rozdział 13ty nie występuje w tekście źródłowym- mimo podejrzanej numeracji, nagranie zawiera pełny tekst. (Summary by Glys)

22565.d: Oswald Forster grows up during the tumultuous years of the early 15th century on the English/Scottish border. Entering the service of Henry "Hotspur" Percy, he travels throughout England, Wales, and Scotland, fighting Glendower and the Welsh, the Bairds and their allies in Scotland, and finally assisting the Percy family in their attempt to overthrow King Henry and re-instate the true heir, thereby beginning the Wars of the Roses. (Summary by Alexandria Adair)

22566.d: Maximilian Harden, the well-known critic, writes in the Zukunft (7th September 1907) of the Historical Miniatures: “A very interesting book, as might be expected, for it is Strindberg’s. And I am bold enough to say a book which should and must be successful with the public. The writer is not here concerned with Sweden, nor with Natural History. A philosopher and poet here describes the visions which a study of the history of mankind has called up before his inner eye. Julian the Apostate and Peter the Hermit appear on the stage, together with Attila and Luther, Alcibiades and Eginhard. We see the empires of the Pharaohs and the Czars, the Athens of Socrates and the ‘Merry England’ of Henry VIII. There are twenty brief episodes, and each of them is alive. So powerful is the writer’s faculty of vision, that it compels belief in his descriptions of countries and men.” “The question whether these cultured circles really were as described, hardly occurs to us. Never has the remarkable writer shown a more comprehensive grasp. Since the days of the Confession of a Fool, Strindberg has become a writer of world-wide significance.” - Summary by from the Preface

22567.d: This novel is a psychological thriller about the travails of a young lady who suddenly finds herself penniless and without a job. She is taken in by a close relative as a secretary, but everything around her is not what meets the eye alone. - Summary by Yoganandh T

22568.d: Written in the 19th century "Celtic Scotland" is an account of the early civil history, ethnology, and complex cultural landscape of ancient Scotland, known as Alban, during the Celtic period.

22569.d: In 1859, Charles Dickens launched his own newspaper, "All the Year Round". Unsurprisingly, Dickens included many short pieces by--guess who? Dickens was a reporter, a flaneur, and an insomniac, all three traits which prompted him incessantly to walk about, and observe. Thirty-seven of these stories he collected under the name of "The Uncommercial Traveller". - Summary by Mark Leder

22570.d: This is the story of Anne Shirley, one of literature’s most memorable characters, a young orphan girl taken in by two middle-aged siblings, Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, at their remote farm in the fictional village of Avonlea, on Prince Edward Island, Canada. Anne’s vivid imagination, excitability, quick wit, and penetrating intelligence challenge their patience but brighten their own lives, as their affection for Anne grows into an abiding love. Published in 1908, this is the first of eight books that follow Anne from the age of eleven through to adulthood, against the backdrop of early 20th century Canadian culture. Ten film adaptations of the books, several foreign films (including an anime version), and a Netflix series, testify to the enduring and universal appeal of Anne Shirley of Green Gables. (Summary by tshoes76)

22571.d: Josiah Flintabbatey Flonatin, esq. explores a bottomless lake in a submarine of his own design in hopes of finding another civilization at the centre of the earth. - Summary by FableSol

22572.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 14 recordings of The Faded Flower by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. This was the Weekly Poetry project for April 26, 2026. ------ Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English poet, literary critic, philosopher, and theologian who was a founder of the Romantic Movement in England and a member of the Lake Poets with his friend William Wordsworth. He wrote the poems “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” and "Kubla Khan". This Weekly Poem was first published in the Monthly Magazine , August 1836. - Summary by Wikipedia

22573.d: The English poet John Milton supported the Parliamentarian side during the English Civil War and publicly defended the execution of King Charles I. He held the post of Secretary for Foreign Tongues in the government of Oliver Cromwell's Commonwealth. The relatively few poems he wrote during this period often reference the political situation of the time. (Summary by Alan Mapstone)

22574.d: In a 1856 Congressional speech, Massachusetts Representative Anson Burlingame projected the first public indication that the North was willing to fight for the preservation of the U.S. Constitution and the abolition of slavery. As historian Heather Cox Richardson wrote in her Letters from an American column …: "Forgotten now, Burlingame’s speech was once widely considered one of the most important speeches in American history. It marked the moment when northerners shocked southern leaders by calling them out for trying to destroy democracy. Northerners rallied to Burlingame’s call, and to the new Republican Party he was helping to build, because he had shown it would stand up for their rights." (Summary by John Greenman & Heather Cox Richardson, with permission)

22575.d: The Black Cat (1895-1922) was a monthly literary magazine, publishing original short stories, often about uncanny or fantastical topics. Many writers were largely unknown, but some famous authors also wrote original material for this magazine. The sixth issue of volume 6 contains the following stories: > How David Came Home, by H. A. Fillmore (Phil More): a homecoming with a tragic ending > Pericles P. Pemberton: Cured, by Jessie Reno Odlin: an advertisement in a paper brings unexpected happiness > The Blue Light on the Mountain, by Paul Crandall: witness a strange incident at the hillside > The Pocket of Goat Island, by Henry Reed Taylor: brave firemen are rewarded with an unexpected find > The Phantom Dromedary, by Henry Adelbert Thompson: is the appearance of the dromedary a sign of impending doom? - Summary by Sonia

22576.d: Orestes, acompañado de su fiel amigo Pílades, arriba a las costas del Ponto Euxino, con el propósito de secuestrar la estatua de Artemisa y llevarla a Atenas para expiar el asesinato de su madre Electra. Allí son capturados por los súbditos del rey Toante y cuando van a ser sacrificados a los dioses Orestes descubre que la sacerdotisa encargada de ejecutar el ritual es...su hermana Ifigenia, a la que todos creían muerta en Áulide por orden de su padre Agamenón para asegurar la navegación a Troya. Los dos hermanos y Pílades elaboran un engaño para escapar del país de los Tauros y regresar a Grecia juntos y con la estatua de Artemisa. El argumento y personajes enlazan con otros tres dramas de Eurípides, siendo éste el último que cierra el ciclo que empezó con "Ifigenia en Áulide" y continuaba con "Electra" y "Orestes" desarrollando las desventuras de los hijos del rey Agamenón, de la dinastía de los Átridas (Introducción por Epachuko)

22577.d: El Marqués de Bradomín, ya viejo y desengañado, recuerda con melancolía su paso por la Corte carlista de Estella, donde entre neblinas, misas solemnes, frailes pintorescos y ecos de guerra, revive el fulgor marchito de antiguas pasiones. Veremos tapices de nostalgia, orgullo herido y belleza crepuscular que envuelve al protagonista en su última luz. Luego de un accidente, la recuperación trae un encuentro amoroso, de desastrosas consecuencias, que será el colofón de sus aventuras. (Introducción por mpinedag) Obras en esta serie: Sonata de Otoño Sonata de Estío Sonata de Invierno Sonata de Primavera

22578.d: Ponza has just arrived in town to take a job as secretary for the prefecture. He lives with his wife, whom no-one ever sees, in an apartment on one side of town and has rented an apartment on the other side for his mother-in-law, Signora Frola, in the same building as the other characters, who all love to gossip and speculate about their new neighbour. But soon, mystery builds upon mystery about the Ponza couple and Signora Frola. Is she mad? Is Ponza? Who is Signora Ponza really? Signora Frola’s daughter or an entirely different woman? Pirandello, in his characteristic way, takes us on a wild and hilarious ride through a lot of speculation, but provides no satisfactory answers. - Summary by Winnifred Assmann

22579.d: A collection of twenty stories featuring ghoulies, ghosties, four-legged beasts and things that go bump in the night. Expect shivers up your spine, the sound of a monstrous howl, and the occasional touch of wonder.

22580.d: The American Bee Journal is the “oldest bee paper in America established in 1861 devoted to scientific bee-culture and the production and sale of pure honey. This issue covers such topics such as Hive and Section Making by James Heddon, A Good Shade for Bee Hives by L. James, state convention reports and correspondence. - Summary by Larry Wilson

22584.d: Nuestra Señora de París, de Victor Hugo, publicada en 1831, es un texto que está considerado como una de las obras más importantes del autor y, al mismo tiempo, una obra fundacional del romanticismo francés. Es también, según se advierte en su título, un homenaje a la catedral de Notre Dame, icono y bastión arquitectónico, religioso y cultural de París y de Francia toda. Acá debemos hacer un alto y mencionar que Hugo fue un denodado defensor del patrimonio cultural de Francia, y que en parte esta novela es una denuncia sobre la desaparición por olvido, descuido y desinterés institucional de iglesias, abadías y castillos. Además, presenta en un excepcional capítulo un contrapunto entre la arquitectura y la invención de la imprenta, desarrollando así la relación tan íntima que hay entre ellas y su efecto en la sociedad, la historia y el progreso de Francia. La trama se desarrolla en París en 1482, cuando era una ciudad de estrechos callejones, de plazas, de patíbulos y de diferentes sectores regidos por distintos señores que administraban los impuestos y la justicia según un criterio propio que aún no se subsumía completamente bajo el poder del rey, en este caso Luis XI. En ese escenario es donde conviven la corte, el clero, los estudiantes y los marginados de la llamada Corte de los Milagros, personajes importantes en toda esta trama y cuya incidencia en la historia merecería un capítulo aparte. Se entrelazan así, en su historia, una gitana hermosa y muy joven, un poeta, un capitán de la guardia del rey, un arcediano poderoso y regidor de la catedral y un deforme campanero llamado Quasimodo. Sus destinos se entrecruzan en una historia de amor cuyo hilo conductor es el amor no correspondido. Fantástica mezcla a la que podemos agregar el poder de la iglesia y de la nobleza, adornado por juicios, fiestas populares, motines y ejecuciones. Es una novela que reflexiona fundamentalmente acerca de lo bello y lo feo, la libertad y el encierro, el amor y el odio, y sobre cómo la sociedad plantea quiénes tienen voz y quiénes quedan relegados al silencio social. A Hugo no le tiembla el pulso para la crítica en este punto y se florea con ella. Por último, hay un personaje que no es humano pero que es una construcción humana y figura como símbolo de todo el conjunto: la catedral de Notre Dame, cuyo significado es indisociable del momento que transitaba la sociedad francesa. (Introducción por Carlos Lombardi)

22586.d: To follow - Summary by Pamela Nagami

22587.d: A Strange Love: A Novel of Abnormal Passion was first published in French as Escal-Vigor in 1899, the English translation nine years later. It is as relevant today as it was a century ago, treating the torture of coming out to oneself, the fear and loneliness of isolation, the high cost of coming out to others, and the high value of personal integrity. The protagonist, Count Henry Kehlmark, is a highly educated heir to a large fortune, nurtured by loving and nearly selfless women. The author gradually reveals Henry’s secret, implied by the title, through a series of insinuations much clearer to the reader than to the other characters, as is fitting in a tragedy. His return to his family estate begins to erode the dearly bought prudence of his boarding-school youth. His finding a talented and like-minded student with whom to share the wealth of his mind leads to crises at home and at last to scandal in the community. Although the age of the lad is eighteen when he meets the count, the author's insistence on a significant age difference between the partners (calling the lad a "child" or even a "little boy") makes the friendship appear much too Greek for our comfort in twenty-first century America. A reader unfamiliar with French needs to know that the second-person singular (thou/thee/thy/ thine) is the intimate form of address; the plural (you/your/yours) is formal. (Summary by T. A. Copeland)

22588.d: My Little Athenian Cousin of Long Ago is about a boy named Hiero growing up in ancient Athens. In the story, he and a boy named Duris grow in friendship while learning about life in the city. Through their friendship, the book shows what everyday life was like for children in ancient Greece, including school, family life, festivals, and important events happening around them. (Summary by Narrator)

22589.d: Often overlooked by history, the first ladies of the United States White House have always been held in high esteem during their time, often hosting state functions, and supporting the president privately and publicly. These are short vignettes of the first twenty-five U.S. first ladies from Martha Washington to Edith Roosevelt. The concluding chapters describe various rooms of the White House and explain Official Etiquette. There is also a special introduction by beloved poet and author Margaret Elizabeth Sangster. - Summary by Larry Wilson

22590.d: Few Americans today realize that Michigan and Wisconsin were once part of French Canada. French influence in the region continued through the eighteenth century, decades after France ceded Canada to Great Britain at the end of the Seven Years’ War in 1763. In this volume, Wisconsin’s French past is recounted by historian Louise Phelps Kellogg. Born in Milwaukee, Kellogg earned her Ph.D. in history from the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 1901, where she studied under the noted historian Frederick Jackson Turner. She spent much of her career at the Wisconsin Historical Society, conducting research and publishing books and articles on the history of the American Northwest. Kellogg begins with the European discovery and early settlement of New France, then gradually shifts attention during the seventeenth century to the western frontier in northern Michigan and Wisconsin. This rugged region became one of the centers of New France’s principal industry; the fur trade with Native American tribes. Through the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, she traces the French dependence on Native alliances, the shifting relationships among tribal groups, and the rivalry between French traders and the Dutch and English merchants of upper New York for trade and influence. The events in this book help to show why French settlement developed so slowly in Wisconsin and the wider Northwest, and partly explain why New France failed to grow as rapidly as the English colonies to the south. Kellogg presents a clear and detailed account of a formative period in the history of the Great Lakes region and early North America. - Summary by Ted Lienhart

22593.d: Rev. John Thompson and Rev. Eleuthera I.D. Pepper were authors in the 19th century holiness movement. Dr. Pepper authored several hymns and edited the “Memorial of Rev. John S. Inskip,” one of the more prominent leaders in the holiness movement. This book offers short devotional thoughts for each day of the year covering the tropics related to holiness, sanctification, and living a life of purity and humility. Each entry has a portion of scripture with brief comments. - Summary by Larry Wilson

22595.d: This story highlights life in a British girls’ boarding school during World War One. The desires of the girls to do something consequential for the war effort are showcased in this book, but demonstrates how easily these innocent desires can be thwarted. While written with young teens in mind, it can be enjoyed by the entire family.

22596.d: Baker presents an objective view of the life of Tiberius Caesar, the second emperor of Rome, and successor to Augustus. While covering the years from age thirteen to the emperor's death, the author considers issues of Augustus' succession, Tiberius' military career, and the challenging political aspects of the early Roman Empire. - Summary by Mark Harrington

22597.d: It is the purpose of this booklet therefore, to bring within the scope of visualization, as nearly as possible, the very essence of relativity, and to state its principles in terms devoid of unfamiliar phrases and illustrations. The popular mind is not satisfied with vague statements, mathematical equations and formulæ. It calls for an explanation in words of every day usage, and where a technical term must be employed then a definition of that term in language simple and lucid. To meet these requirements without sacrificing scientific accuracy has been the earnest endeavor of the author. - Summary by William F. Hudgings Narrator’s note: This book has been read as written although it contains several factual errors, e.g.: confusing photons with electrons and using an incomplete formula for acceleration due to gravity.

22599.d: The first half of this volume of The Remembrance of Things Past describes the narrator's grief at the flight of his mistress Albertine; he learns of her death in a riding accident; his feelings for Albertine alternately intensify and diminish, and at length his memories of her fade. The narrator's article is at last published by Le Figaro, and at the same time he meets his old flame Gilberte, whose mother Odette had been married to the late Charles Swann and is now the wife of M. de Forcheville. Thanks to a bequest from an uncle, Gilberte is now a rich heiress. The narrator then renews relations with Albertine's friend Andrée, from whom he learns more about Albertine. The narrator makes his long-postponed trip to Venice with his mother. The volume ends with news of the marriage of Robert de Saint-Loup to Gilberte. - Summary by Michael O'Kelly

22602.d: A story of social class and personal ambition as the young woman Minnie navigates her relationships. [Better summary to come.] - Summary by Cathy Howell

22603.d: The Magic of Jewels and Charms" is an early 20th century semi-academic work Dr. Kunz examines the historical significance, folklore, and mystical properties attributed to precious stones and gems. He explains the superstitions, symbolism, mysticism, religious significance, crystal gazing and birth stones, exploring their roles in various cultures as talismans, amulets, and objects believed to confer magical powers. - Summary by LynneT

22604.d: The author, Margaret Elizabeth Sangster, is the grand daughter of the beloved poet and hymn author Margaret Elizabeth (Munster) Sangster. At fifteen she was a staff writer for The Christian Herald, and then became the youngest overseas correspondent during World War I for them, and wrote a column for The Christian Herald for fifty years. She was editor an contributor to numerous periodicals including Cosmopolitan, Redbook and McCalls, and authored many novels. She wrote a poem a day for a syndicated column for sixteen years. This collection of her poems spans topics of love, home, nature, faith, war, and a final group written from the viewpoint of France at the end of World War I. (Summary by Larry Wilson)

Also included are a number of composers you have probably never heard of. (Summary by The Reader)

22608.d: Mother Earth, an American anarchist journal, was self styled as "A Monthly Magazine Devoted to Social Science and Literature". Mother Earth was initiated in 1906. Its first editor was Emma Goldman, an activist in the United States. Contemporary activists and writers in Europe as well as the US contributed to its pages. In addition, it contained essays by historic figures. This is Volume 1 of the series. (Summary by Christine Rottger)

22609.d: Lummis presenta Los exploradores españoles del siglo XVI como una defensa apasionada de la labor colonizadora española en América. Sostiene que los exploradores del siglo XVI han sido injustamente menospreciados y busca corregir ideas erróneas sobre ellos. Relata su propia investigación y viajes, mostrando admiración por figuras como Colón, Cortés y Balboa. Afirma que sus hazañas transformaron el conocimiento del Nuevo Mundo y merecen un reconocimiento más justo en la historia contemporánea - Summary by mpinedag

It is unabashedly proselytizing, arguing that the perspective offered by the author, a white Christian American man, should be disseminated to the country's young people with the goal of producing a generation of parents who would raise obedient, monogamous children. - Summary by Rick Whitaker

22611.d: The Scientific American may be the oldest continuously published periodical in the United States, having launched its first publication in 1845. It has been a mainstay of popular science with in depth articles across a broad spectrum of scientific fields. In this supplement are short articles ranging through such topics as "The Living Jerboa in the Zoological Garden of Berlin," "The Eruption of Krakatoa," "The Military Engineer and His Work," and, "Action of Caustic Soda on Wood." - Summary by Larry Wilson

22612.d: Nuts in Family Meals: A Guide for Consumers by US Department of Agriculture is a guidebook for anyone searching for unique ways to use nuts in a variety of different recipes. From purchasing nuts, to preparation and storage, this book offers valuable resources and steps to creating the best meals to be consumed with family, friends, or on one's own.(Summary by favorezeanuna)

22613.d: Young d'Artagnan travels to Paris to make his fortune as a King's Musketeer. He befriends Athos, Porthos, and Aramis, three Musketeers each with a past to hide. Fiercely loyal to King and Queen, they get themselves mixed up in court intrigue to prevent Cardinal Richelieu's machinations against Queen Anne. Who is the mysterious "Milady" who seems in such high favor with the Cardinal? Who was Athos, and why is he always depressed? Where does Porthos get his money, and why did Aramis abandon the Church for the world? Find out that and more in the first installment of the Dramatic Readings series of the d'Artagnan Romances, starring Alexander as d'Artagnan, Weretortoise as Athos, Jim Hedrick as Porthos, and Alexandria Adair as Aramis. - Summary by Alexandria Adair

22614.d: Damon, a Syracusan senator, is to be beheaded for treason, but the new king permits a general, Pythias, to pledge his own life for his friend to allow him to visit his wife and child before his execution. His motives are mixed, considering that Pythias's popularity with the masses could pose a threat to the king’s power, and he does expect the friendship to survive this test. This book is a novelization of a silent film, a fairly common practice in the ’10s and ’20s, and the film was based on John Banim’s 1821 play of the same name. Some stills from the movie are included in the text source link. Although the writing does not meet the highest editorial standards, the characters are well developed and the plot both well paced and plausible. The reading experience is an emotional workout. Whatever you may expect to find in this story, you are almost certain to find more than you bargained for. (Summary by Thomas Copeland)

22615.d: The Rev. Andrew Gray, the author of the following Sermons, was born about the year 1630. Before he had reached the age of twenty, his extraordinary gifts and graces secured his entrance on the office of the Christian Ministry; and he died, after labouring for about two years in the work of winning souls to Christ. From one so young, and, therefore, in man's judgment, so inexperienced, we are scarcely prepared to expect either the riches of a matured intellect, or the tokens of much growth in grace. But "none teacheth like God," and the name of Andrew Gray is now enrolled, and will continue to be so, as long as godliness continues to be cultivated, among those who are sometimes led to maturity in grace ere ordinary men have left the rudiments of religion. - Summary by William King Tweedie

22617.d: Gwendolyn B. Bennett was a poet, short story author, journalist and educator. These poems were published from 1923 to 1927. - Summary by Newgatenovelist

22621.d: Rothert, a local historian, studied the notorious Ohio and Mississippi river basins and the pirates and highwaymen who operated there in the period following the Civil War. - Summary by LynneT

22622.d: The Middle Ages! They seem so far away; intellectually so preposterous, spiritually so strange. Bits of them may touch our sympathy, please our taste; their windowglass, their sculpture, certain of their stories, their romances, - as if those straitened ages really were the time of romance, which they were not, God knows, in the sense commonly taken. Yet perhaps they were such intellectually, or at least spiritually. Their terra - not for them incognita, though full of mystery and pall and vaguer glory - was not the earth. It was the land of metaphysical construction and the land of spiritual passion. There lay their romance, thither pointed their veriest thinking, thither drew their utter yearning. Is it possible that the Middle Ages should speak to us, as through a common humanity? Their mask is by no means dumb: in full voice speaks the noble beauty of Chartres Cathedral. Such mediaeval product, we hope, is of the universal human, and therefore of us as well as of the bygone craftsmen. Why it moves us, we are not certain, being ignorant, perhaps, of the building's formative and earnestly intended meaning. Do we care to get at that ? There is no way save by entering the mediaeval depths, penetrating to the rationale of the Middle Ages, learning the doctrinale, or emotionale, of the modes in which they still present themselves so persuasively. - Summary by Preface

22623.d: Household Words was an English weekly magazine edited by Charles Dickens in the 1850s. It took its name from the line in Shakespeare's Henry V: "Familiar in his mouth as household words." The subject matter was varied, including poetry, fiction, non-fiction and opinions. - Summary by Lynnet

22624.d: Literatura Americana es una colección de ensayos en la que Batres Jáuregui examina el desarrollo intelectual del continente desde la época colonial hasta el siglo XIX. El autor destaca cómo la literatura americana surge primero bajo la influencia española, adquiriendo gradualmente voz propia conforme las nuevas naciones buscan identidad cultural. Batres analiza figuras clave, movimientos literarios y las tensiones entre la tradición europea y las aspiraciones americanas. También subraya el papel de la historia política —independencias, repúblicas jóvenes, conflictos internos— en su formación literaria, criticando y a la vez defendiento el valor cultural. (Introducción por mpinedag)

22625.d: Stephen Duane and his friend Chuck are chemists working on a weapon to end WWII when the experiment is interrupted and something goes wrong. Waking to a new world where Earth has been conquered and every understanding they posses about civilization has been uprooted. This story is an adventure in the concepts of honor, power and identity. Join Steve and Chuck as they navigate a new world and re-visit their longest held beliefs. (Summary by Cindy Morton)

22626.d: "The School and Society" by John Dewey is an educational work published in 1899. Based on three influential lectures, it establishes a foundational framework for progressive education that responds to the Industrial Revolution's transformation of childhood learning. Dewey argues that modern schools must replace the practical, hands-on education children once received working alongside parents. He proposes making collaborative experimentation central to schoolwork, designing student-centered classrooms around children's natural interests rather than passive listening, and integrating manual training with academic subjects to reconnect theory with meaningful practice. - Summary by Project Gutenberg

22627.d: Meditations on the Twenty-Third Psalm: Dr. Jones is one of the greatest of living preachers, and on both sides of the Atlantic, his splendid gifts are fully recognized. - Summary by The Publishers Weekly 1922

22628.d: "This book is not addressed to the learned, or to those who regard a practical problem merely as something to be talked about. No profound philosophy or deep erudition will be found in the following pages. I have aimed only at putting together some remarks which are inspired by what I hope is common sense." Bertrand Russell opens the preface with this statement of the intended audience, goals, and writing style of The Conquest of Happiness. The "recipes," as he calls this collection of personal anecdotes, self-reflection, and advice, are written as a wise mentor or elder might share them. As I previewed the text to understand the book's character and how it wanted to be read, it revealed itself to me as a forerunner of the modern self-help genre. Russell was an academic, philosopher, and mathematician who set out to write this in an accessible, commonsensical style. Published in 1930, this book contains outdated generalizations that are unmistakable products of its time, and the 21st Century listener or reader may find the characterizations of gender, cultural, and class roles pretentious, tone-deaf, dismissive, and awkward. Yet, many of the observations of human nature and causes of unhappiness and happiness are profoundly relevant today: attention-culture, comparing ourselves to our peers, seeking chronic stimulation, aversion to boredom, and conflating constant excitement with happiness. The central thesis of the work gradually reveals itself: Self-absorption and preoccupation are causes of unhappiness. While happiness does come from within, the happy person cultivates it through directing their attention outwards, joyful engagement with the people and world around them, and hobbies and interests as sanctuary against inevitable losses and setbacks. As Russell observes, “to be happy in this world, especially when youth is past, it is necessary to feel oneself not merely an isolated individual whose day will soon be over, but part of the stream of life.” I hope The Conquest of Happiness positively shapes your perspective and journey. - Summary by Bryan Travis

22629.d: It’s 1925, and Sam Dodsworth has just sold his successful automobile company and set off on a European vacation with his wife, Fran. Sam expects to spend a few months traveling before returning to business, but Fran becomes enamored with European culture, and unhappy with small town life, favors staying in Europe permanently. Sam and Fran are forced to reassess both their lives and future marriage. Lewis’ satirical novel was later adapted for the stage, film and musical theater. - Summary by The Narrator

22630.d: Kull, a barbarian from Atlantis, has conquered the land of Valusia and now rules over it as king. Little does he know that an ancient race of serpent people are using magic to replace humans with serpent men, and now seek to seize his kingdom. Can Kull battle the serpent people invasion? And if he does, how can he tell ally from foe? Can the power of the sword defeat the evils of sorcery? - Summary by Klaatu

22631.d: Sixteen-year-old pretty, golden-haired Nancy Drew wishes to help the Turners, who are struggling relatives of the recently deceased Josiah Crowley, by finding a missing will that can give them claim to Crowley's estate. Aided along the way by friend Helen Corning, she becomes interested in the case because she dislikes Crowley's snobbish nouveau riche social-climbing heirs presumptive, the Tophams. - Summary by Wikipedia

22632.d: Although the radio boys in this case are but creatures of the author’s imagination, nevertheless they are typical of all the men who have taken part in bringing radio to its present stage. Even Marconi himself likes to take pride in the assertion that he too was at one time an amateur, because he insists that during his early experiments he was only a boy amateur tinkering with a little known subject. - Summary by Jack Binns

22633.d: In this 12th installment of The Rover Boys, the story follows the Rover brothers—Dick, Tom, and Sam—as they break from daily school life to visit the family farm. The boys engage in some last minute pranks and some contemplation of their futures before leaving Putnam Academy and heading to the family farm. As their luck would have it, the trip is not all rest and relaxation. They find themselves caught up in a localized mystery involving missing family horses, hidden mountain caves, and freight thefts. - Summary by afutterer

22634.d: The Rev. Alfred J. Church, who has made a good reputation by his stories of life in the Biblical and classic world, adds to his laurels by a fresh volume entitled 'The Burning of Rome.'. It is a story of the days of Nero, and shows how the Christians and pagans lived and thought, and how the new religion gradually displaced the old in the minds and hearts of converts. The basis of the narrative is the historical writing of Tacitus, and Mr. Church's ambition seems to lie in close adherence to the probabilities. He has studied minutely the letters of Paul the Apostle, and seeks wherever practicable to link together the names of persons in the Epistles to places and incidents in Roman history. Epicharis, the chief character, is somewhat idealized. The story is moderately exciting, and may be recommended to Sunday-school libraries, and to all who would know how the Christians lived in the days when there was civilization but no Christian church edifices. - Summary by The Critic, 1891

22635.d: The Black Cat (1895-1922) was a monthly literary magazine, publishing original short stories, often about uncanny or fantastical topics. Many writers were largely unknown, but some famous authors also wrote original material for this magazine. This is issue number 7 from volume 6 with the following stories: > A Delilah of the Cinder-Path, by Samuel Scoville, Jr.: what reward will await the athlete at the end of the race? > A Touch of Nature, William Forster Brown: a prisoner of war has an unexpected stroke of luck > Jefferson Simms; his Exits and Entrances, by Henry Adelbert Thompson: a whole town is hell-bent on following this one man > The Footsteps of Fear, by Fanny Kemble Johnson: no one can stop death from creeping nearer > A Thousand-Dollar Job, by Richard Barker Shelton: why would a seemingly harmless action be worth so much money? - Summary by Sonia

22636.d: Literary, Biographical, Historical - Summary by Subtitle

22637.d: I have ventured to offer this small work to the public with the view of accomplishing two objects; first, to endeavour to impress upon the reader's attention the constituted differences of evidence which exist in the various departments of human knowledge, to which the higher kinds of reasoning are applied; and, secondly, to avoid as much as possible those crabbed and technical words and phrases, so profusely scattered over most of our elementary as well as popular treatises on Logic. The first object, that of pointing out the differences in the evidence on which various subjects rest, must be allowed by all to be an important one. Many errors in judgment, in matters of great interest to mankind, take their rise from vague and incorrect notions as to the nature of the subjects which come under the mind's contemplation. And in regard to the constant use of antiquated terms, in works which professedly aim at the strengthening and guiding of the understanding, we are fairly entitled to conclude that such terms ought to be limited to the smallest possible number, to prevent a gloomy and mysterious air being given to that, which, in other respects, might be considered as both pleasant and perspicuous. I have avoided, as far as possible, all controversial matter. When a subject on which there still exists a diversity of opinion has crossed the path of my inquiries, I have unqualifiedly adopted the principles of one party; not with the most distant idea of pronouncing a dogmatical verdict on the question at issue, but solely from the wish to prevent the reader's attention from being drawn to topics which have only a remote connexion with the general principles of reasoning. - Summary by Preface

22638.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 16 recordings of A Woman's Love by Arthur Conan Doyle. This was the Weekly Poetry project for May 24, 2026. ------ Sir Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle was a British writer and physician. He is best known for his four novels and fifty-six short stories about the fictional consulting detective Sherlock Holmes and his assistant Dr. Watson, which are milestones in crime fiction, and for his first work featuring Professor Challenger, The Lost World (1912), which gave its name to a subgenre of speculative fiction. He was a prolific writer who produced over 200 stories and articles, four volumes of poetry, and a number of works for the stage. He was knighted by King Edward VII in the 1902 Coronation Honours. - Summary by Wikipedia

22639.d: Ce recueil, compilé par l'helléniste français Émile Legrand, rassemble une trentaine de petits contes grecs, traduits sur les textes originaux. Comme souvent dans la tradition folklorique d'origine orale, ces récits varient entre anecdotes moralistes, incidents humouristiques et vignettes tragiques. - Summary by Sonia

22641.d: This is a collection of 33 poems read in English by LibriVox volunteers during September 2026.

22642.d: A founding tale of the American heartland, Giants in the Earth tells the story of three families of Norwegian pioneers who make their way in covered wagons to the Dakota Territory in 1873. Per Hansa, his wife Beret, and their fellow settlers struggle to plant their first crops, care for each other during the harsh winters, cut tunnels through the snow to keep the cows fed, endure plagues of locusts and crop failures, and gradually coax a living from the vast prairie. Per Hansa is doggedly optimistic and dreams of endless progress; Beret is overwhelmed by her terror of the endless open spaces. Their experience reveals the human cost paid by the immigrants who opened the American West. The novel is the first in a trilogy and is based on the author’s own experiences as a settler as well as the those of his wife's family, who had been immigrant homesteaders on the American prairie. (Summary by tshoes76)

22643.d: Betty Shaw is chosen as a companion to a wealthy lady. But her life becomes shrouded ln mystery and intrigue from the day she sets foot in that house - Summary by Yoganandh T

22644.d: “Beware what you wish for – you may get it!” These words may have been written for Victor Frankenstein, a proud young man of Switzerland who thought he had the elements of a chemical giant within himself. After some months of feverish work in isolation, he succeeded in creating and animating an actual giant, a homunculus. Afraid to confront the being, Frankenstein left it to its own devices. Spurned in horror by every human it revealed itself to, beaten and wounded, what was it to do? It locked one thought within its grotesque brain: find its creator, and make him pay! - Summary by Mark Smith

22645.d: Intent on locating a missing professor, Todham Todd, the boys visit a strange series of caves. - Summary by ClueChaser

22647.d: Newlywed Juliette Magill Kinzie moved from her home in Connecticut to the newly built Fort Winnebago in central Wisconsin in 1830. Her husband, John Kinzie, the son of a fur trader who had grown up on the frontier, had recently been appointed by the federal government as an Indian sub-agent to the Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) people. The couple lived near Fort Winnebago, close to the present-day city of Portage, Wisconsin, until 1833, when they moved to Chicago. These memoirs focus primarily on the two years Juliette Kinzie spent in the Wisconsin wilderness. She devotes considerable space to the difficulties and dangers she encountered while traveling across Wisconsin to places such as Chicago and Fort Howard (now Green Bay). The Kinzies were frequently in the company of local Indians, and the author recounts many observations and experiences with them. One of the highlights of the memoirs is her account of the Black Hawk War of 1832. In addition to describing her own experiences, she devotes two chapters to the 1812 Battle of Fort Dearborn (Chicago), as witnessed by her husband and mother-in-law.. - Summary by Ted Lienhart

22648.d: Hannibal, like Napoleon, towers over all the figures of an age of war in its grandest aspects, and of the shock of nations in conflict. We possess hardly anything which has emanated directly from this extraordinary personage, scarcely a phrase, not a line of correspondence; his achievements and character are described by bitter enemies. Yet through the mists of calumny and detraction we can see the form and the lineaments of that gigantic figure, one of the most commanding that has appeared in history. - Summary by Adapted from the Preface

22649.d: This short book follows John Henderson, who, for one reason or another, feels betrayed by a cult. He sets out to get his revenge. (Summary by Simon Evers)

22650.d: Rutherford, a theologian and minister, argues that rulers are subject to the law and not above it. Previous to the authorship of Lex Rex the guiding principle was Rex Lex, the idea that kings are the law and that arbitrary rule was acceptable. After the publication of the book, Rutherford faced the charge of treason and Lex Rex was subject to book burnings. - Summary by progressingamerica

22651.d: Household Words was an English weekly magazine edited by Charles Dickens in the 1850s. It took its name from the line in Shakespeare's Henry V: "Familiar in his mouth as household words."
