22652.d: The boys prepare to graduate from high school and are witnesses to a suspicious airplane emergency landing. Soon they become involved with their father, the famous detective Fenton Hardy, in investigating a theft ring only to be falsely accused and arrested. Bailed out by wealthy individuals that the boys had solved mysteries for in the past, the intrepid duo sets about to solve the thefts and clear their names. - Summary by James R Hedrick

22653.d: Century Readings in Greek and Latin Literature in Translation propose to call to the reader's attention practically every significant figure in the literary experience of Greece and Rome from Homeric times to the fall of the Empire in the West and to the fading of the Eastern Empire into Byzantinism. They include as much as possible of the travel background that so effectively contributes to reality in literature; Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece, many parts of the Roman Empire, are vividly glimpsed, and the city of Rome is illuminated from many sides. They present much that is of universal interest in regard to religion, philosophy of life, statecraft, and criticism, and occasional significant paragraphs of historical or antiquarian interest. They are prefaced by brief literary appreciations; it is too often forgotten that the classics are not only documents, but the inspired product called art. They are purposed above all to present the classics in their human appeal. Men in movement in the tragedy and comedy of life, men in reflection on the vicissitudes, the follies, the nobilities, the contradictions, the absurdities, the futilities, of life, men in the earnest endeavor to solve the problems of belief and conduct: this is the stuff of the ancient classical literatures, and interest in this has been the guide in the selection of these readings. In the choice of translators, the general principle as to form has been that verse is best reproduced by verse and prose by prose; of the exceptions, some are due to the lack of adequate verse, some to the special excellence of the prose, some to convenience. As to the transfer of content, those translations have been chosen which seemed best to unite substance and spirit in an attractive unity. Not always is the most recent translation, nor even the most scholarly, the best reproduction. Century Readings in Greek and Latin Literature may perhaps claim to be something more than a compilation. Their character is the result of much traveling in the Realms of Gold; at first with the guidance and companionship of honored masters in the classics, George Lincoln Hendrickson, Alexander Kerr, Moses Stephen Slaughter, and Charles Forster Smith, and afterward in the paths to which they pointed the way. It is the result of many actual travelings in ancient classical lands and in lands familiar to the ancient classical peoples, and of years of sojourn in Eternal Rome. It is the result of twenty-five years of instruction in the classical tongues, and of lecturing to classical and non-classical students on life, letters, and the fine arts, always with the painful lack of a single easily accessible volume for illustration or for study in course. It has been determined by personal and actual need, and thus in a measure partakes of the nature of organic growth. - Summary by Introduction

22654.d: “Yes, he was the most beautiful Prince that ever was born. Of course, being a prince, people said this; but it was true besides. When he looked at the candle, his eyes had an expression of earnest inquiry quite startling in a new born baby. His nose—there was not much of it certainly, but what there was seemed an aquiline shape; his complexion was a charming, healthy purple; he was round and fat, straight-limbed and long—in fact, a splendid baby, and everybody was exceedingly proud of him, especially his father and mother, the King and Queen of Nomansland, who had waited for him during their happy reign of ten years—now made happier than ever, to themselves and their subjects, by the appearance of a son and heir.” (Chapter 1) So begins the story of the little lame prince, who loses his mother and is dropped on a marble staircase on his christening day, paralyzing his legs. His father dies soon after, and his uncle exiles him to rule in his place. But his fairy godmother comes to the rescue, giving him a magic travelling cloak to make sure he grows up to become a wise and thoughtful king, despite all his misfortunes. - Summary by Dinah Maria Mulock Craik and Winnifred Assmann

22655.d: Shortly after the slaughter at Cullodden moor, Andrew Boyd, son of a wealthy landowner, frees a fugitive Scot of higher degree from a mishap, and he and his father hide him from his English pursuers in their venerable old Scottish home called Windlestrae. Because the of the Boyds’ English roots, their neighbors suppose them to be loyal to King George, a mistake that makes their home relatively safe for their guest, but a troop of English soldiers, with a highland captive, stray to Windlestrae in the fog at night and make themselves at home there. The stage has been set for a tense domestic drama, which gradually develops into an adventure calling for quick wits, cool daring, and iron resolve. (Summary by Thomas Copeland)

22658.d: In 1916, three prominent identities in the Sydney art world - Sydney Ure Smith, Bertram Stevens and Charles Lloyd Jones - got together to publish Australia's first art magazine. Their aim was to make the work of Australian artists known to the Australian public, and, through high quality reproductions, to give an idea of its quality to those who were unable to see the originals. All of the 102 issues of Art in Australia, published between 1916 and 1942 have now been made available, complete with illustrations, on the National Library of Australia's Trove web site. The third issue of the magazine consisted mainly of short biographical sketches of contemporary Australian artists, including Norman Lindsay and Blamire Young, illustrated by examples of their work. Anticipating a speedy end to World War 1, this issue also included an optimistic piece on the role of art and design in the industrial development of post-war Australia. - Summary by Phil Benson

22666.d: The Monster of Grammont is a mystery thriller novel by British author George Goodchild, set in a haunted French château where a mysterious "monster" terrorizes the inhabitants, leading to murder and a complex investigation by a visiting sportsman, Ralph Wallace, and his companion, Connie Conrad, who uncover secrets involving the château's owners and staff. The book blends traditional country house mystery elements with interwar European settings. - Summary by Gerald Moe

22667.d: In the third and final installment of his autobiography, John G. Paton tells of his travels through America and Britain speaking about and raising money for missionary work in the New Hebrides. He brings his readers up to speed on the work God had done up to that point through missionaries in the New Hebrides and shares about the needs for ongoing work. May his autobiography continue to challenge us to follow our ever-faithful God with greater devotion and to share His good news with those who have not heard. As Paton says in the conclusion to this book, "Should the record of my poor and broken life lead any one to consecrate himself to Mission work at Home or Abroad that he may win souls for Jesus, or should it even deepen the Missionary spirit in those who already know and serve the Redeemer of us all—for this also, and for all through which He has led me by His loving and gracious guidance, I shall, unto the endless ages of Eternity, bless and adore my beloved Master and Saviour and Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever." 22668.d: Luis E. Pacheco nos entrega una ficha bibliográfica y, sobre todo, genealógica del héroe nacional de Colombia, Francisco José de Paula Santander. En un estudio detallado, nos familiarizamos con los parientes en línea recta y los parientes políticos de Santander, personajes del siglo XIX. Este es un trabajo que realza la figura del prócer y proporciona honor al legado del llamado "Hombre de las Leyes" y "Organizador de la Victoria". (Introducción por mpinedag)

22669.d: By 1889, when A Marriage below Zero appeared, very few English novels had been published that contained even a hint of homoeroticism. The Picture of Dorian Gray appeared the next year, in 1890. It is not, then, surprising that the secret at the heart of Alan Dale’s story dares not speak its name. Readers, on the other hand, would have been at least dimly aware of the nature of the husband’s secret because of the conventions of fiction, where only details strictly relevant to either texture or plot are mentioned. Real life, on the other hand, is nothing but texture; there is no plot, and therefore details that are later recognized as having been significant are not noticed when they occur. The fast friendship of two men need not be perceived by a naive young woman as the cause of their being shunned by their social peers, but with these matters spotlighted by an author, even before “closet,” “outing,” and “LGBT” had become part of daily speech, any reader must have seen a connection. The goal of the plot is to lay bare what was then considered an unmentionable, almost inconceivable vice. The plot consists of a gradual peeling away of the veneer masking the husband’s infidelity, with the injured wife remaining one step behind the reader throughout. To appreciate the dramatic irony generated by this process, modern readers, who will be already five steps ahead of the wife, must adjust their powers of insight to see the story from the point of view of the original audience, bearing in mind that some women at that time could be completely ignorant of sexual intercourse itself. Indeed, there is no evidence in the novel that the betrayed wife even knew enough about sex to realize that married couples engaged in any greater intimacy than passionate kissing. Even when she finds herself on the verge of full knowledge, she does not realize that her husband's condition is a matter of his innate nature rather than simply of behavior, but he does. At this point, the story's interest shifts from wife to husband, and the reader begins to see the entire story from his point of view—as a desperate experiment that has gone tragically awry. (Summary by Thomas A. Copeland)

22670.d: „Mutter!..“ von Heinz Tovote ist ein psychologisch-feinfühliger Roman über Freundschaft, Identität, Mutterliebe und die oft schmerzhaften Widersprüche zwischen Ideal und Wirklichkeit. - Summary by Microsoft CoPilot

This collection of four plays was published by Louisa MacDonald as a resource for other families to put on the same kind of entertainments. The four plays are: Cinderella, or the Glass Slipper Beauty and the Beast Snowdrop The Tetterbys - Summary by Devorah Allen

Harben: a story of greed and crushed hopes > The Luck of William the Angel, by Paul Shoup: who can save Rosalind from an unwanted marriage? > The Warden's Overcoat, by Grace Gorrill Gowing: follow a prisoner in his escape > The Trade Rat Mine, by Eustace V. Bray: how a prospector stumbled unexpectedly onto gold - Summary by Sonia

22673.d: This work is a collection of stories centered around boys and girls who expressed deep devotion to their faith in the late 17th century. They showed spiritual depth and passionate love for Jesus. As you listen, you will journey into themes of salvation, moral lessons, and what it means to have child-like faith. - Summary by favorezeanuna

22674.d: Household Words was an English weekly magazine edited by Charles Dickens in the 1850s. It took its name from the line in Shakespeare's Henry V: "Familiar in his mouth as household words." The subject matter was varied, including poetry, fiction, non-fiction and opinions. - Summary by LynneT

In 1876, Chadwick published his first book of poems and would continue to write poetry over subsequent decades. He was also a prolific author of books, producing over 30 in his lifetime. They consisted of his sermons and other theological writings (which were published in a series), historical and biographical monographs, and volumes of poetry. - Summary by Wikipedia

22678.d: This is the second Ellery Queen novel, wherein the writer turned sleuth works with... or sometimes in opposition to... his father, an inspector in the New York Police Department. The scene is French's Department Store, renowned for its exclusive merchandise until a body turns up on display in its window. - Summary by LynneT

22679.d: Science fiction is a genre encompassing imaginative works that take place in this world or that of the author’s creation where anything is possible. The only rules are those set forth by the author. The speculative nature of the genre inspires thought and plants seeds that have led to advances in science. The genre can spark an interest in the sciences and is cited as the impetus for the career choice of many scientists. It is a playing field to explore social perspectives, predictions of the future, and engage in adventures unbound into the richness of the human mind. - Summary by A. Gramour

22680.d: Etienne Lantier (our line to the Rougon-Macquart Cycle) goes to work as a coal miner in the Northern France town of Montou. Conditions are terrible, and inevitably, the miners go on strike, with dire results. - Summary by Mark Leder

22682.d: This exciting adventure is the first to take place outside the Hardy boys' well-known town of Bayport. The boys travel to the Great West in search of a forgotten treasure. - Summary by ClueChaser

22683.d: This is the light-hearted account of the author's trip cross-country, with his wife and small child, from New York City to San Francisco, in a 'flivver', slang for a small, inexpensive, and often somewhat undependable car (in this case, a model-T Ford). Despite dire predictions from friendly advisors before departure, the trio enjoy 37 days of travel, camping, while getting a better view of 'real America'. - Summary by Mark Harrington

22684.d: History of the Great American Fortunes by Gustavus Myers is a landmark early-20th-century critique of how immense wealth was accumulated in the United States. First published in three volumes between 1909 and 1910, the book examines the rise of powerful American fortunes—from colonial landowners to railroad magnates and industrial monopolists such as the Astors, Vanderbilts, Morgans, and Rockefellers. He portrays America's great fortunes not as heroic tales of entrepreneurship but as case studies in systemic injustice, revealing how economic power was amassed not through ingenuity alone but through fraud, exploitation, land grabs, political influence, and manipulation of laws and finance. Myers contends that economic inequality was built into the structure of American capitalism, producing concentrated wealth alongside widespread poverty and labor exploitation. - Summary by Celine Major

22685.d: Louis Klopsch was a German-American journalist and publisher, whose most enduring work was the first “red letter” edition of the Bible. Notably he took over The Christian Herald magazine and with Thomas De Witt Talmage as editor greatly extended its circulation. His fund raising campaigns through the Herald raised millions of dollars for relief of Russian famine victims and relief of famines in India. In 1895, Klopsch purchased the floundering Bowery Mission in Chicago and as president turned it around financially. Other works by Louis Klopsch include Daily Light on the Daily Path, a book of daily prayers, and he edited and published A Budget of Christmas Tales by Charles Dickens and others. His broad reading is exhibited in this volume of quotations from a broad range of authors including Shakespeare and Dryden, Longfellow and Burns, Pythagoras and Aristotle, and the Bible, and dozens of others. These quotations are arranged by several hundred topics from Ability and Absolution to Worship, Youth, and Zeal. But then there is Grumbling, Kisses, Poetry, Preaching, Sleep, War, and more. - Summary by Larry Wilson

22686.d: In the absence of ancient castles and mansions, Australia has its own gothic tradition which often uses remote rural settlements as sites for hauntings and other strange happenings. This collection of uniquely Australian gothic tales reflects urban Australia's fear of the bush, and its sense of horror at the brutalities of the colonial enterprise. - Summary by Phil Benson

22687.d: Cowper is the most important English poet of the period between Pope and the illustrious group headed by Wordsworth, Byron, and Shelley, which arose out of the intellectual ferment of the European Revolution. As a reformer of poetry, who called it back from conventionality to nature, and at the same time as the teacher of a new school of sentiment which acted as a solvent upon the existing moral and social system, he may perhaps himself be numbered among the precursors of the Revolution, though he was certainly the mildest of them all. As a sentimentalist he presents a faint analogy to Rousseau, whom in natural temperament he somewhat resembled. He was also the great poet of the religious revival which marked the latter part of the eighteenth century in England, and which was called Evangelicism within the establishment, and Methodism without. In this way he is associated with Wesley and Whitefield, as well as with the philanthropists of the movement, such as Wilberforce, Thornton, and Clarkson. As a poet he touches, on different sides of his character, Goldsmith, Crabbe, and Burns. - Summary by Goldwin Smith

22688.d: In case any of my brother ministers should think of discoursing on the subject of this book, a word or two may be prefixed on the literature. The whole moral system of AQUINAS (Secunda Secundae of the Summa) is built on this framework; and a marvellous structure it is, well worthy of the attention of all who wish either to sharpen their logical faculty or to widen their view of the moral world. - Summary by Preface

22690.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 18 recordings of Vision by Marjorie Pickthall. She was once "thought to be the best Canadian poet of her generation." According to The Canadian Encyclopedia "From an early age [Pickthall] contributed stories to the magazines and newspapers; and before her first book appeared, her genius was recognized". - Summary by Wikipedia

22691.d: Huck Finn, der Held des wahrscheinlich bekanntesten Jugendbuchs von Mark Twain erschien 1884 - acht Jahre nach dem "Tom Sawyer". Der obdachlose Huck Finn, Sohn eines trinksüchtigen Herumtreibers gilt wohl zu Recht als das Original des Genres "Punk". Er wächst im asozialen Milieu auf, läßt sich nichts sagen von Erwachsenen, schon gar nicht von etablierten Respektspersonen. Die Abenteuer und Fahrten des Huckleberry Finks schildern die Entwicklung Hucks , die an das Ende des "Tom Sawyer"anknüpft. Eine spannende und humoristische Schilderung - wieder (wie beim "Tom Sawyer" mit Happyend (Befreiung des Sklaven Jim, Annäherung des Chaoten Huck an das bürgerliche Leben. (Zusammenfassung von Jos van Aken)

22692.d: Young Scottish doctor visits and has dangerous adventures with smugglers and emotional interactions with villagers amongst the Cornish mines in Cornwall. (Summary by JenNoel)

22693.d: Old Fentiman has displayed the impropriety of dying in the Club, and Murbles’ fastidious attention to detail brings to question the line of inheritance of not one, but two legacies. After fighting the Spanish in Europe as a young man, Peter Blood settled in Somerset, to recover from his war wounds and open a medical practice. Unfortunately, he became entangled in the ill-fated 1685 Monmouth uprising against King James II. After the King’s troops defeat the rebels, the latter are tried for treason. On arrival in Barbados, Dr Blood and his fellow slaves were sold at auction to traders and plantation owners. Blood was purchased by a certain Colonel Bishop, along with a former shipmaster, Jeremy Pitt, and a yeoman farmer, Andrew Baynes. Blood’s skills as a physician win him several small freedoms and he also gains the sympathy of Arabella Bishop, niece of his owner. Taking advantage of a Spanish attack on Bridgetown, Peter Blood and his fellow convicts, escape into a life of piracy and freedom on the waters of the Caribbean. In 1838, when he was twenty, he escaped to Delaware and eventually made his way to New York and then to Massachusetts. As a free man, Douglass became one of America’s greatest voices for the ideals which gave birth to the country, in part by repeatedly pointing out that those ideals were not being extended to him. His speech in Rochester, New York, on July 4, 1852, is a timeless reminder of the failings, and the promises, of America. - Summary by Tom Shoesmith

Drawing on his contacts, the author is able to tour a royal palace, visits harems, and gets an invitation to a wedding at the home of a wealthy Jewish family. He also leads readers through the labyrinthine bazaars of Tunis, observes proceedings at the Bey's court, and provides an insider's account of the country's rather medieval government and penal system. Part 2 chronicles the author's travels through the remarkably varied Tunisian countryside to provincial towns including Bizerte, Kairouan, and Sfax. During his travels he visits desert oases and lives briefly in a Bedouin community, describing their lives, customs, and self-government. (Summary by Ted Lienhart)

22780.d: The following work is presented to the public as the last literary composition which its well known author lived to complete; and it contains the result of various observations, made by a vigorous and cultivated mind, upon different subjects of taste and literature. It was concluded a very short time previous to his decease; it assisted in cheering and engaging his mind, in soothing the languor of declining health, and in recalling the delightful remembrance of former associates, and of a long course of intellectual pursuits. To his friends these circumstances will render the work additionally valuable. They will, from the natural and best feelings of the human heart, cherish the relic which reminds them of those hours of social conversation when subjects of literature were discussed; when they were illuminated by his scientific and enlightened mind, or exhilarated by his innocent and undissembled cheerfulness. The public, we trust, will receive the Work as the last performance of an author whom they have long approved, of one whose life was uniformly devoted to their, and his own, best interests: those of science, and literature; of religion, and virtue. - Summary by Preface

22782.d: This is the story of Wooden Leg, one of sixteen hundred warriors of the Northern Cheyennes who fought against Custer at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. Wooden Leg tells of growing up on the Great Plains, Cheyenne courtship, camp life, spirituality, and hunting; of skirmishes with other Tribes; and of the Cheyennes’ valiant resistance against the army of the United States. Wooden Leg recalls the fight against Custer at the Little Bighorn, a recollection that stands as the first published Native account of that battle. Wooden Leg related the story in interviews with Thomas B. Marquis, formerly an agency physician for the Northern Cheyennes. Marquis checked and corroborated or corrected all points of importance with other Cheyennes. - Summary by Barry Eads

22792.d: Joseph C. Lincoln was a prolific author who wrote many short stories and novels centering on life in a fictionalized Cape Cod. 22793.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 14 recordings of The Meeting Waters by Elizabeth H. Whittier. 22794.d: Set in England during the reign of King Henry VIII, this story follows young Miles Paton and his family through the upheaval surrounding William Tyndale and the translation of the Scriptures into English. Author Emma Leslie uses charming and simple historical fiction to acquaint her readers with Church History, and to make these important times accessible to any age. (Summary In-Progress) - Summary by Luella Margaret

22795.d: „Little Dorrit“ ist ein Roman von Charles Dickens. Die Erstausgabe erschien - wie so oft bei den Werken von Dickens als Fortsetzungsroman zwischen 1850 und 1852 Dorrit, das jüngste Kind der Familie Dorritt, die im Marshalsea-Gefängnis für Schuldner in London geboren und aufgewachsen ist. (Summary by josvanaken)

22796.d: The U. S. Navy Cook-Book is a guide published by the United States Naval Institute. Unlike many cookbooks, this one provides recipes and techniques for cooking for large groups. This Second Edition was published in 1920.- Summary by TriciaG

22797.d: Published in 1921, this book recounts the exploration of the Canadian Northwest and the history of the region's fur trade. Drawing heavily on the firsthand accounts of the explorers themselves, the author also enriches the narrative with observations from his own extensive travels and with stories gathered from trappers and gold prospectors. In addition to describing the hardships and achievements of the explorers, the book offers glimpses of Indian life, including buffalo hunts, as well as the daily work and living conditions of the region's trappers. - Summary by Ted Lienhart

22798.d: Robert Louis Stevenson published the novel "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" in 1886. A first dramatic version came out on stage in 1887, and a second in 1888. A new adaptation - this offering - was made in 1897 by Luella Forepaugh and George Fish (soon to become Mr. and Mrs. Fish in 1899), and this melodramatic adaptation became the version used, with screenplays by Forepaugh and Fish, for at least two early movie versins of the story. - Summary by Todd H-W

22799.d: ...A high-powered mystery of strange and evil happenings in the nation's capital! - Summary by Front cover

22800.d: "The Greek Way" is an immersive and provocative exploration of Ancient Greece, viewed through the lens of the great thinkers, writers, and poets of that eminent society. Hamilton begins with an exploration of the mind-spirit duality of human nature, and its contrasting manifestations in the cultures of the East and West. She then proceeds to illustrate the unique character of Greek genius in all the ancient world. Starting with the Periclean age, and proceeding to future generations, she paints a living portrait of the Greeks in their heyday, and beyond. Familiar with the language of ancient Greece, she provides ample quotation of Greek poets and playwrights, which she uses to compare against Greeks of other generations, as well as artists of more recent times. Beauty in simplicity, love of nature and of life with all its faults, and awareness of one's place in the human world, are all exemplified in the selections chosen by Hamilton, which she uses to supplement this insightful history. Summary by E. Sharp

22801.d: Lilian Leland was a vivacious, courageous, petite young American woman 25 years of age, who by diary and letters to her friends and family, wrote this lively travelogue wherein she described how she, with her father's business connections and support, embarked upon a solo journey of nearly 60,000 miles around the world, which lasted for nearly two years (late 1880's). She visited well known tourist attractions today, which were comparatively primitive at the time she visited them -- for example, reaching Yosemite by stage coach on dirt roads, years before it became a National Park, visiting remote Japanese temples that no white woman had ever seen, visiting China just as the Communist revolution was taking place! Get ready for many lively glimpses of yester-year! Lillian was, by all accounts, a liberated woman not bound by the conventions of her time. Her mother, Mary A. Leland, was one of the first women to study medicine in the U.S. and lectured on anatomy as early as 1852. Her father, Theron C. Leland, was a popular writer, lecturer, reporter, freethinker, and secretary of the Liberal League. Leland married H. L. Andrews, the son of famous abolitionist and freethinker, Stephen Pearl Andrews.

22802.d: A collection of tales from the folklore of Southern India. - Summary by Beeswaxcandle

22803.d: Al margen de su faceta como político, historiador, escritor y periodista, es en la de orador donde destaca enormemente Castelar por su elocuencia. Magistralmente plasmada en este texto biográfico de Lord Byron, dibuja su figura, su atormentada vida, palabra por palabra, enlazando en perfecta cronología cada uno de los pasos que el poeta británico dió por tantos lugares de la Europa del siglo XIX. Todas y cada una de las páginas están penetradas de un estilo casi poético donde manifiesta su admiración hacia «El héroe romántico» a quien no duda en atribuirle la categoría de genio. Construye una biografia, cargada de largas, aunque bellísimas frases, encaminadas a reflejar un personaje digno de admiración. Lord Byron vivió intensamente, sintió de un modo profundo, escribió de forma tan apasionada que tanto su gran obra como su vida reciben aquí de manos del escritor español lo que considera como justo y necesario reconocimiento. (Introducción por LU)

22804.d: Jalna is the first book in a series of 16 novels written between 1927 and 1960 by the Canadian writer Mazo de la Roche. It has been adapted for both stage and screen, including Jalna , the 1935 film from director John Cromwell; The Whiteoaks of Jalna , a 13-part mini-series produced in 1972 by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; and Jalna , a 1994 French-Canadian adaptation in 8 parts. A sprawling family saga that spans the century from 1854-1954, it tells the story of the Whiteoaks family of southern Ontario. Jalna is the name of their fictional manor house on the shore of Lake Ontario, named after a British garrison in the Indian city of Benares (Varanasi). It is modelled after a house in Mississauga, Canada, built in the 1850s for a retired officer of the British army, in which de la Roche lived as a child. Billed as Canada’s answer to The Forsyth Saga , the series recounts the conflicts and romantic entanglements of the wealthy and eccentric Whiteoaks. Beginning with the establishment of Jalna in 1863, the narrative revolves around sharp-tongued Grandma Adeline Whiteoak, the 99-year-old matriarch who dominates the family, and Renny, the eldest grandson, striving to bring order the family’s internecine battles and chronic financial instability. Considered a classic in Canadian literature, de la Roche continued to tell the family’s story through her finale in 1960, Morning at Jalna . The 16 novels do not form a sequence, and each can be read as an independent story with at least 6 prequels preceding the “first” novel, which won the inaugural Atlantic Monthly’s $10,000 Book Award when the author was 48. In addition, de la Roche was a prolific author of children’s stories, plays, short stories, and romantic fiction until her death. 22805.d: Torquemada en la hoguera es la obra que inicia la tetralogía de Las novelas de Torquemada. Según algunos académicos el personaje más elaborado de la producción galdosiana. Luis Cernuda llega a afirmar de esta primera novela, “acaso sea para mí la obra máxima de Galdós”. La mejor introducción de esta obra nos la da el propio Galdós en la primera frase: “Voy a contar cómo fue al quemadero el inhumano que tantas vidas infelices consumió en llamas”. Aunque pudiera parecer simplemente una novela de costumbres con espíritu cómico donde se expone a Francisco Torquemada el avaro, el usurero, el despiadado, Galdós nos hace conectar con el personaje y acceder a su psicología a través de su tragedia personal. Su hijo pequeño, Valentín, un prodigio de talento al que Torquemada profesa un enorme amor de padre, cae gravemente enfermo. Ver a su hijo a un paso de la muerte le empuja a buscar la reconciliación con la humanidad y con un Dios al que nunca prestó atención. Es tal su torpeza y su mezquindad en el entendimiento de la justicia divina que hasta los más pobres se apiadarán de él. Otras novelas de la serie: Torquemada en la cruz (en preparacion) Torquemada en el purgatorio (en preparacion) Torquemada y San Pedro (en preparacion) (Introducción por gabrielledo)

22807.d: Hill presents us with a vivid scholarly account of how one ambitious, visionary Spanish administrator, carved a new province out of the untamed northern frontier in the mid 1700s. The author traces Escandón’s rise from soldier to colonizer, showing how his mix of military discipline, political acumen, and pragmatic alliances with Indigenous communities allowed him to establish dozens of settlements across what is now South Texas and the State of Tamaulipas. This is one of those histories that feels small in scope but big in significance, revealing how a single person's decisions rippled across centuries of borderland identity, in an area that nowadays, over 6 million people call home. - Summary by mpinedag

22808.d: Household Words was an English weekly magazine edited by Charles Dickens in the 1850s. It took its name from the line in Shakespeare's Henry V: "Familiar in his mouth as household words." She highlights the region’s diversity—from bustling modern cities to Indigenous traditions that shape daily life—while emphasizing the shared challenges and aspirations that connect Latin American nations. Trade, economy, education, and the impending WWII impact is reviewed in macro terms, ending with encouraging words to the reader and the governments to work together for the benefits of the American Continent.. - Summary by mpinedag

22823.d: The author of this gothic tale was one of the first Union soldiers to lose his life in the Civil War. His semi-autobiographical novel focuses on a young traveler, Robert Byng, who, returning to New York from many years abroad, occupies an absent friend’s flat. With the assistance of an old mentor, he saves the life of a reclusive painter on the floor above him. A close friendship ensues. Byng courts Emma Denman, a beautiful heiress whose intellectual sister has disappeared, presumed drowned. His mentor, who admired the lost woman and believes her to be still alive, travels to Europe to seek her. Meanwhile, Byng fraternizes with one of the other passengers on the ship on which he arrived, an accomplished older man, named Densdeth, of questionable character. The relationships among all of these individuals constitute a mystery whose solution becomes increasingly imperative. (Summary by Thomas A. Copeland)

22824.d: A descendant of New England witches, Boston socialite Martha Klemm finds herself drawn to the occult. She hypothesizes that while there is evil in this world its presence is as natural as good and it cannot be absolute. She supposes that a solitary get away to a "haunted" island will facilitate her meditation on the notion of evil. - Summary by Brian Fullen

22825.d: The Castaways of Disappointment Island is the true story of Charles Eyre, who in 1907 was working as apprentice sailor on the Dundonald, a British four-masted steel barque. Caught in a storm, the Dundonald sank after hitting the rocky coastline of a tiny subantarctic island known as Disappointment Island which lies 500 km below New Zealand. Many died in the wreck while the survivors had no choice but to wait, hoping for a passing steamship to rescue them. For seven months, they subsisted on mollymawk flesh, seal meat, seaweed and "root", as they spent the winter wearing barely any clothes in a climate where fog rarely lifts, sun seldom shines and where torrents of rain left them soaked to the skin. - Summary by Barry Eads Link to the museum where some of the castaways artifacts are on display: https://www.canterburymuseum.com/explore/collections/castaways-and-coracles .

22827.d: Stories (including some really adventurous ones) from a missionary in India. (More complete summary to come later). - Summary by Aletheia Charis

22828.d: The children Don and Joyce spend their summer vacation on their grandparent's farm. As Joyce reflects: "I was happy every minute, even when the old turkey gobbler was chasing me around the tree. But what I liked best was to sit out on the porch in the evenings, and listen to the katydids and whippoorwills, and watch the stars come out one by one. And then it was so nice to sit close to Grandma's old rocking-chair and listen to her stories about the Hive of Busy Bees". - Summary adapted from Ending Narrator: Louise Jaeschke Grandma: Patty H Joyce: ShrimpPhish Don: Alexandria Adair Grandpa: Larry Wilson Minor role(s) performed by: , Jenn Broda , InTheDesert , mleigh

22829.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 16 recordings of By Rapids in Love by William Krafts. This was the Weekly Poetry project for August 2, 2026. ------ Our Weekly Poem this week is taken from Specimens of American Poetry. 1829. Edited by Samuel Kettell (1800 - 1855). - Summary by David Lawrence

22830.d: History of the Great American Fortunes by Gustavus Myers is a landmark early-20th-century critique of how immense wealth was accumulated in the United States. First published in three volumes between 1909 and 1910, the book examines the rise of powerful American fortunes—from colonial landowners to railroad magnates and industrial monopolists such as the Astors, Vanderbilts, Goulds, Morgans, and Rockefellers. He portrays America's great fortunes not as heroic tales of entrepreneurship but as case studies in systemic injustice, revealing how economic power was amassed not through ingenuity alone but through fraud, exploitation, land grabs, political influence, and manipulation of laws and finance. Myers contends that economic inequality was built into the structure of American capitalism, producing concentrated wealth alongside widespread poverty and labor exploitation. - Summary by Celine Major

22831.d: The Emigrants is a family saga of Norwegian farmers who settle in North Dakota in the late 1800s. The author paints a loving portrait of a large cast of characters, all different but hoping to make a better life in America. Their early years are hard, living in sod huts and breaking their fields with teams of oxen. They are torn between their homesickness for Norway and their love for the traditions of their homeland, and their growing appreciation that they and their children have become Americans. The novel is a companion to O. E. Rolvaag’s Giants in the Earth, which focused on the settlers as immigrants to America; Bojer’s interest is with the same Norwegian pioneers as emigrants from Norway. - Summary by Tom Shoesmith

22832.d: Eight supernatural and spooky tales that include the spectres of the beyond! - Summary by Patty Harden

22833.d: What happens when you suddenly awaken into a form that is not your own? Gregor Samsa must ponder this question when he wakes up as a creature, and through this new appearance, he must handle the new reality of a bug’s life with both his family and his job. But are they willing to understand his plight? This classic novella of Franz Kafka is presented in a dramatic reading. - Summary by Patty Harden

22834.d: The beautiful and witty Harriet Byron writes to her family about her new acquaintances in London, including the odious Sir Hargrave Pollexfen who attempts to carry her off against her will. Harriet and her rescuer, the titular hero, fall in love, but he is already engaged to another woman. - Summary by nealaa

22835.d: Around the World with Uncle Sam; or Six Years in the United States Army "A true story of travel and adventure by a former enlisted man of the ranks in the U.S. Army. Beginning with recruit life soldiering in Colorado, in the war with Spain, campaigning in Cuba, at Battle of El Caney, capitulation of Santiago; later, traveling across the great American continent, sailing across the Pacific, in the Philippines, a year in China during Boxing trouble, through the Suez Canal, a great storm on the Atlantic, completing the tour of the world. 22836.d: A humorous and philosophical examination of the game of golf, exploring why this deceptively simple sport exerts such a powerful psychological and emotional hold over its players. For in that land at the Earth's core, under the eternal day of the Central Sun, his terrific talents were needed just to stay alive—let alone to fulfill the mission that had called him there! - Summary by Original text

Otis writes that taxation attempts are not constitutional in accordance with law and destructive of the Empire's unity. He also argues that special privileges such as trial by jury, protection of a subject's property, and respect for the natural rights of subjects must be honored. - Summary by progressingamerica

22843.d: Dieses Buch mit dem Titel "Aus den Tiefen des Weltmeeres" ist ein Auszug aus dem gleichnamigen umfangreichen Werk des Zoologen und Tiefseeforschers Carl Chun über die erste größere deutsche Expedition zur Erforschung der Tiefsee. Es ist Teil der populärwissenschaftlichen Reihe "Wissenschaftliche Volksbücher für Schule und Haus", herausgegeben von dem Bremer Reformpädagogen Fritz Gansberg. Im Jahr 1898 brach der zum Forschungsschiff umgerüstete ehemalige Postdampfer Valdivia unter der wissenschaftlichen Leitung von Chun zu einer Forschungsreise auf, die die Erkundung der Tiefsee zum Ziel hatte. Die gesamte Reise erstreckte sich über etwa 32.000 Seemeilen und führte von Hamburg ausgehend über den Atlantik und um Afrika herum in den Indischen Ozean. Das vorliegende Buch befasst sich mit dem Teil der Reise, welcher durch die Gewässer der Antarktis führte. Der Herausgeber verfolgte in seiner pädagogischen Arbeit das Ziel, bei den SchülerInnen das Interesse am Unterricht durch die Ansprache des Gefühls und die Anregung der Phantasie zu wecken. Ganz in diesem Sinne bekommen wir in diesem Buch Eindrücke von der Forschungsarbeit und den dazu verwendeten eigentümlichen Gerätschaften. Wir begeben uns auf die Suche nach verschollenen Inseln, fahren durch das knirschende Packeis und an gigantischen Eisbergen vorbei und besuchen den Lebensraum von Pinguinen und Seeelefanten sowie Eilande voller seltsamer Tier- und Pflanzenwelt. In dem Buch sind Verweise auf Abbildungen enthalten, welche hier zur besseren Lesbarkeit weitgehend weggelassen wurden. Die Fotos können in der unten verlinkten Online-Ausgabe angeschaut werden. (Zusammenfassung von Claus Misfeldt)

22849.d: Science fiction is a genre encompassing imaginative works that take place in this world or that of the author’s creation where anything is possible. The only rules are those set forth by the author. The speculative nature of the genre inspires thought and plants seeds that have led to advances in science. The genre can spark an interest in the sciences and is cited as the impetus for the career choice of many scientists. It is a playing field to explore social perspectives, predictions of the future, and engage in adventures unbound into the richness of the human mind. - Summary by A. Grammour

22850.d: In this, the 14th volume of his Rougon-Macquart cycle, Emile Zola depicts the life struggles of an artist, Claude Lantier--the elder brother of Etienne Lantier ("Germinal"). The book describes his genius, his struggles both to complete his works, and his failure at gaining acceptance, and his tragic end. Because he felt Lantier was in some measure based on him, the artist Paul Cezanna, a lifelong friend of Zola, broke off their friendship permanently. - Summary by Mark Leder

22851.d: In this quick read, Annie Payson Call provides common sense techniques for properly resting the whole body including your overachieving mind. Summary by Christine Rottger

22852.d: Dies ist die Fortsetzung des Romans "Die drei Musketiere". D'Artagnan, Athos, Porthos und Aramis finden sich nach zwanzig Jahren der Trennung wieder zusammen, um neue Abenteuer zu bestehen. 22853.d: William Morris's translation of Beowulf beautifully showcases the unique character of English alliterative verse in one of the finest epic poems of the Middle Ages. The language and syntax employed by Morris is at times challenging, however, it can be a very rewarding reading experience that gives a close adaptation of the original both in language and feel. While written in Modern English, Morris shifts his vocabulary to be heavily Germanic and often archaic. In particular, Morris tends to use the closest cognate words available in Modern English even if the word has long fallen out of regular use. While this was certainly a bold choice that sometimes comes at the cost of readability, the effect achieved is well worth it. This translation is recommended for readers who are already familiar with Beowulf and/or other Medieval literature. It is also recommended to refer to the text while listening to the audio. An effort has been made on the part of the narrator to achieve approximately correct pronunciations of Old English words in the text, however, some minor inaccuracies may be present. (Summary by Taylor Whitehead)

22854.d: OUR CHURCH, HER CHILDREN AND INSTITUTIONS is a three-volume illustrated Catholic reference work edited by Henry Coyle, Theodore Mayhew, and Frank S. Hickey, published by Angel Guardian Press in Boston in 1908. Volume 1 focuses on the work of the priesthood, Catholic family life, home life, prayer practices, and moral guidance. It includes advice on attending Mass, praying, living the Catholic ideal, and the role of the Catholic home. (Summary by rroderick)

22855.d: Young Tim, whose father is disappointed in him, forms a close friendship with an older boy, for whom his father conceives a strong dislike. A four-year difference in age prevents the boys from maintaining a close friendship at Eton but does not diminish their affection. When the older boy graduates and discovers the girl of his dreams, he unbosoms his love agonies to his childhood confidant. To appreciate Tim's response, a reader must realize, as Tim himself begins to do when his friend is leaving Eton, that his love for him is, as the narrator suggests, "wonderful, passing the love of woman." The sexual component of this emotion, although obscure to the child, is apparent to his tutor, who ignores “much of what he knew, and the whole of what he suspected." (More than this oblique acknowledgment of homosexuality, especially in the case of a child, could scarcely have appeared in print in 1891.) The focus of the later chapters shifts between Tim’s damaged relationship with his father and his awkward new relationship with his rapidly maturing friend, until they are harmonized in a bittersweet ending. (Summary by Thomas A. Copeland)

22857.d: This is the third collection in the Mini Multilingual Bedtime Stories series, featuring short Aesop's fables in English, Chinese, and Spanish. These brief animal stories share timeless moral lessons in a gentle, bedtime-friendly style. - Summary by LydiaX

22858.d: A contemporary critic said of Among the Mongols by James Gilmour, "Robinson Crusoe has turned missionary, lived years in Mongolia, and wrote a book about it." James Gilmour's account of some of his experiences in Mongolia and his explanations of Mongolian culture are certainly an interesting read. From the one meal a day eaten by Mongols to the proper means of approaching a tent so as not to be eaten by dogs, from the Mongol justice system to their version of Aesop's fables, 19th century Mongolia was a fascinating place. Among the Mongols lets us travel across time and space to catch a glimpse of this other way of life so foreign to us. (Summary by AletheiaCharis)

22859.d: Each of four complete strangers receives one quarter of a treasure map from an anonymous source. They are then invited to share and share alike in the recovery of a fortune. Why? 22861.d: Thus have I written the history of King Arthur and of sundry of those knights that comprised his Round Table. For so may you see with what patience, what labor and what self-devotion those knights served their king, their Round Table and their fellows. For those knights were very gallant gentlemen who thought but little of care and trouble and who practised self-denial when that self-denial could be of avail to help their friends or to benefit the world. For ever they brought aid to those who were in trouble and comfort to those who were afflicted ever they brought food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty; and ever they destroyed giants and monsters and wicked men, and so made the world a better and a comelier place in which to dwell. And wit ye that no man can do better than that in this world: to bring aid to the afflicted; food to the hungry, and a release from trouble to those who are in anxiety. Yea; for seven years have I been engaged in writing these books, which contain the history of these things. Many other things have I done in that time. For I have painted many pictures besides having written these books and other works of a like sort. And these books are four in number: first, there is the Book of King Arthur; then there is the Book of the Champions of the Round Table; then there is the Book of Sir Launcelot and his companions, and now there is this Book of the Grail and the Passing of Arthur, and this book is the last. For those books comprise a history of all this time; for though there be many things left untold in them, yet those things are of small consequence. For all that is of greater note hath been here told, and that in full. And I thank God that he hath permitted me to finish this work, for wit ye that when a man taketh seven years of his life to complete an undertaking, he knoweth not whether he shall live to complete that which he hath begun. But so I have completed it, and for that I thank God who permitted me to complete it. Amen. - Summary by Authur

22878.d: Cavanagh of Kultann is a historical romance set in British India’s northwest frontier (on the border of present day Pakistan and Afghanistan) at the end of the nineteenth century where the honest and upright district officer, Richard Cavanagh, struggles to perform his administrative duties in the face of political tensions and intrigue during a worsening epidemic in a poverty-stricken outpost of the empire. His efforts to alleviate the suffering of the people under his jurisdiction are thwarted by a meddling British politician and competing political interests including among local Pashtun and Pathan. The novel presents a vibrant vision of life in British India and how it contrasts with London society. Core themes are loyalty, duty, race relations, the strength of friendship between men and the threat women were perceived to present to the masculine frontier community. Cavanagh’s search for love is marred by an early scandal during a furlough in London leaving him bereft of hope of finding true love. Will Richard Cavanagh ever achieve personal redemption? The author, Joan Sutherland (Joan Maisie [Collings] Kelly, 1890-1947) was a popular British novelist and singer who travelled widely. Cavanagh of Kultann, published in 1911, was the first of over 40 novels, many of which were set in territories colonised by Britain. - Summary by KiwiReader24

22888.d: Every minister ought to read Matthew Henry entirely and carefully through once at least. You will acquire a vast store of sermons if you read with your note-book close at hand; and as for thoughts, they will swarm around you like twittering swallows around an old gable toward the close of autumn. If you publicly expound the chapter you have just been reading, your people will wonder at the novelty of your remarks and the depth of your thoughts, and then you may tell them what a treasure Henry is. He is most pious and pithy, sound and sensible, suggestive and sober, terse and trustworthy. You will find him to be glittering with metaphor, rich in analogies, overflowing with illustrations, superabundant in reflections. He delights in apposition and alliteration; he is usually plain, quaint, and full of pith; he sees right through a text directly; apparently he is not critical, but he quietly gives the result of an accurate critical knowledge of the original fully up to the best critics of his time. He is not versed in the manners and customs of the East, for the Holy Land was not so accessible as in our day; but he is deeply spiritual, heavenly, and profitable; finding good matter in every text, and from all deducing most practical and judicious lessons. - Summary by Charles Spurgeon

22889.d: Avonturen van kabouters Gnoom en Kobold samen met de andere wezens in het bos. Wie zich misdraagt wordt een lesje geleerd. De vijf hoofdstukken vormen een doorgaande verhaallijn, maar zijn evt. ook los van elkaar te lezen.

22890.d: Whiteoaks (aka Whiteoaks of Jalna) is the second book in a series of 16 novels written between 1927 and 1960 by the Canadian writer Mazo de la Roche. It has been adapted for both stage and screen, including Jalna , the 1935 film from director John Cromwell; The Whiteoaks of Jalna , a 13-part mini-series produced in 1972 by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; and Jalna , a 1994 French/Canadian adaptation in 8 parts. A sprawling family saga that spans the century from 1854-1954, it tells the story of the Whiteoaks family of southern Ontario. Jalna is the name of their fictional manor house on the shore of Lake Ontario, named after a British garrison in the Indian city of Benares (Varanasi). It is modelled after a house in Mississauga, Canada, built in the 1850s for a retired officer of the British army, in which de la Roche lived as a child. Billed as Canada’s answer to The Forsyth Saga , the series recounts the conflicts and romantic entanglements of the wealthy and eccentric Whiteoaks. After introducing the history of Jalna, the first novel described the tumult of the post-war years, and revolved around sharp-tongued Grandma Adeline Whiteoak, the 99-year-old matriarch who dominates the family, and Renny, the eldest grandson, striving to bring order to the family’s internecine battles and chronic financial woes. In Whiteoaks , Adeline dies shortly after her hundredth birthday, leaving the entire family squabbling over her hoarded fortune. Considered a classic in Canadian literature, de la Roche continued to tell the family’s story through her finale in 1960, Morning at Jalna . The 16 novels do not form a sequence, and each can be read as an independent story. Attesting to its success, the first book won the inaugural Atlantic Monthly’s $10,000 Book Award when the author was 48. In addition, de la Roche was a prolific author of children’s stories, plays, short-stories, and romantic fiction until her death - Summary by ASharma

22905.d: No valid reason exists for writing about political thought in the sixteenth century except that there actually are people who desire to know how men thought in those days. But there are quite good reasons for that desire. The thought of the men of those days was ultimately concerned with questions no more satisfactorily answered now than they were then; and with questions that are, or may become, as practically important to us as to them. It may be that the assumptions with which their thought started are so unlike the assumptions we make, as to disable us from seeing their arguments and conceptions as other than fallacious and mistaken. So much the worse for us, I am inclined to say, if that be so. But even though their reasoning do not help us to solve their problems for ourselves, yet it is surely true that we can learn something from it of use to ourselves. We may learn, perhaps, to realize the extent to which conclusions depend upon assumption. We may learn to realize how many irreconcilable views may rationally be taken on the same question. We may perhaps learn, if we need to do so, to doubt our own possibly too glib assurances. If the old thinkers raise doubts in our minds on fundamental questions, that is all to the good. If they help us to see how much is involved in our own assumptions, that is all to the good. It is good for us, too, to have questions that puzzle us stated in terms to us unfamiliar. We may even learn to see the thought of our own passing moment as a thing as ephemeral as theirs. But unless we study their thought without any sort of prejudgement, we shall be unlikely ever to understand them. And if we come to it with an assumption of superiority, or a notion that the problems that perplexed them have by us been solved, then we are likely to get no good of it at all. - Summary by Introduction

22906.d: In 1917, events in Russia dominated global headlines as World War I gave way to revolution and communists seized control of the country. As the war dragged on, the public watched their worst fears about socialism come to life. To help readers make sense of the unfolding chaos, publisher H.W. Wilson commissioned editor Clara Manning to compile a timely collection of magazine articles capturing every side of the crisis and Russia's path to revolution. - Summary by Ted Lienhart

22911.d: Jacob Riis was a Danish photojournalist whose groundbreaking book documented the lives and struggles of working people – many of them immigrants – in New York in the late 1880s. His narrative is sensitive but unsparing, and filled with intimate portraits of the men, women, and children of America’s Gilded Age underclass. With both camera and pen, he showed the nation children sleeping under East River piers, fathers crippled by lead exposure, mothers desperate to feed their children, husbands and wives doing piecework in dark tenement rooms, and gangs of “toughs” cycling in and out of prison. Riis’s photographs and vivid prose brought home to a largely ignorant middle class the problems of overcrowding, child labor, and exploitation of working people in America’s growing cities. His work influenced housing reform, sanitation efforts, and broader Progressive Era activism, and helped establish photojournalism as a powerful tool for social change. (Summary by Tom Shoesmith)

22922.d: “Modeste Mignon” is one of Balzac’s last novels, first appearing in 1844 with a revised edition in 1846. Modeste, the central character, is described as “well-born, well-educated, and right-minded.” Using a pseudonym, she initiates secret correspondence with a famous poet. That poet cynically brushes off her advances and allows his secretary to answer in his place. Romance — based on these masked identities — blooms, but complications arise when Modeste’s family suddenly comes into a fortune. Readers of other works by Balzac will recognize familiar themes: Romantic idealism, calculations based on money and social class, and provincial versus Parisian manners. They may, however, be surprised by the author’s tender attention to the richness of Modeste's character. Recent critics have come to appreciate Balzac’s development of this young female protagonist who asserts (what we would now call) “agency” in her own life, refusing to be a mere commodity in the marriage market. (Summary by Bruce Pirie)

22928.d: The materials for a biography of Lactantius are very meagre. He was more occupied in study and writing, than in the scenes of active life; and consequently, the incidents are but few. He was born in the third century, not far from the year 250. There is no information as to the place of his birth... But as he was educated at Sicca, in Numidia, under Arnobius, a distinguished teacher of rhetoric, the conclusion is more probable that he was born in Africa. From Nicomedia he was called, at an advanced period of life, into Gaul, by Constantine the Great, to be preceptor of his eldest son, Crispus, who had already been advanced to the rank of Cesar in the imperial government, and was regarded as the presumptive heir of the empire...As Crispus was much occupied with the cares of government, the labors of Lactantius, in his honorable position, could not have been very regular, nor pressing. According to Eusebius, however, they met with an ample return, in the excellent character which they formed, or fostered, in Crispus... He lived to a good old age, and died about the year 325, probably at Treves, which was the capital of Gaul, and had been the residence of Crispus. Lactantius is known to us mainly as an author. The works of his which have come down to our day, are mostly religious treatises of a philosophical character, the aim of which was, to sap the foundations of the heathen religion then prevalent in the Roman empire, and to vindicate the religion of Christ. It is from this point of view that he ought to be judged; for however defective, or erroneous even, in some respects was his conception of Christianity, it was not so much his purpose systematically to exhibit its doctrines, as favorably to impress intelligent pagans in regard to it, and to confirm, in those days of trial and persecution, the wavering faith of many professed disciples of Jesus. For this work he seems to have been eminently qualified. His reading was very extensive, particularly of authors, both in prose and poetry, in whose works the current moral and religious principles were presented, either systematically or more incidentally. To such authors he refers with much copiousness and facility, and turns them to account, by showing their coincidence with dis own views, or by exposing their errors. Besides his ample stores of learning, which could not but ensure him respect, the familiar acquaintance which he possessed with the works of the best writers, and the intellectual habits which, as a rhetorician, he was led to cultivate, secured for him the advantages of an attractive style of writing. A Treatise on the Anger of God [is written] in opposition to the Epicurean dogma, that the Supreme Being exercises neither anger, nor favor, towards men, but is wholly indifferent to their concerns; and to the doctrine of the Stoics, that is God is only merciful, to the exclusion of anger. - Summary by Christian Review - September 1845

22929.d: W. E.B. Du Bois, one of the greatest voices of the American experience, was born just after the end of the Civil War, was the first black American to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard, founded the NAACP in 1909, and lived to the beginnings of the modern civil rights movement in the early 1960s. In the middle of his long life, he published Darkwater: Voices from Within the Veil, a deeply thoughtful reflection on how black Americans were still struggling under the weight of Jim Crow and backlash from Reconstruction. He writes lyrically on the common bonds of working-people, the importance of education and the care of the nation’s children, and considers the future of American democracy, recently challenged by the surveillance, repression and racial discrimination of the Wilson Administration, the strains of the First World War and the widening inequality of the post-war boom. Du Bois died in 1963, and was honored by then-Vice President Lyndon Johnson during the March on Washington, the same event at which Dr. Martin Luther King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech. The book is considered the first of Du Bois's three autobiographies and was followed by Dusk of Dawn: An Autobiography of a Race Concept, and The Autobiography of W. E. B. Du Bois: A Soliloquy on Viewing My Life from the Last Decade of its First Century. - Summary by Tom Shoesmith

22935.d: History of the Great American Fortunes, Volume III by Gustavus Myers is the concluding volume of Myers’s three-part examination of how enormous fortunes were accumulated in the United States. Myers portrays the growing concentration of capital as being supported by corruption and favorable legislation, while ordinary citizens and workers bore much of the economic cost. - Summary by Celine Major

22936.d: The Crisis is the official publication of the NAACP first published in 1910 with W. E. B. Du Bois, one of the founders, as editor. He exercised almost total control of the content and opinions of the publication until he resigned in 1934. Du Bois was one of the most ardent advocates for total civil rights for all racial minorities and was a prolific author for the cause. From Du Bois’ editorial: “The object of this publication is to set forth those facts and arguments which show the danger of race prejudice, particularly as manifested to-day toward colored people. It takes its name from the fact that the editors believe that this is a critical time in the history of the advancement of men.” This issue features articles such as, "The Assault on Mr. Washington," "The Fight for Liberty in St. Lucia," "The National Association of Colored Women by A.W. Hunton," and, "My Little Love Salome," a charming poem by L.A. Proctor. - Summary by Larry Wilson

22951.d: In an elm-shaded street in a near-by town there stands a pleasant house. In that house there is a library, and in that library, hidden away in a safe place, there is a little worn book covered with faded brown leather. It is the pocket diary of a brave man who crossed the Great Plains with an ox-team in the early days of the California gold rush. Its pages are yellow with age, the ink is pale, and the writing is so fine that one almost needs a magnifying-glass to read it. Here in as few words as possible are recorded some of the episodes and adventures of this terrible journey. ... The route followed by the Twins is the same that is traced so carefully in this diary, and many of the incidents and events of their journey are authenticated by some note or statement in the record. - Summary by Foreword

22958.d: This audiobook covers Volume 2, Books XX-XXXI, of The Spirit of Laws (originally published as “De l’esprit des lois”). Despite facing censorship, Montesquieu’s works, especially this one, were extremely influential in the Western world. He was the most quoted authority on government by American founding fathers, second only to the Bible. Catherine the Great and the Declaration of the Rights of Man also heavily drew from Montesquieu’s theories on separation of powers. Having laid out much of his theory of ideal government in volume 1, Montesquieu devotes this portion to discussing examples and implications. He examines the interplay among religion, economy, and law throughout history, along with an investigation of how laws are made. At the end, Montesquieu tacks on his views on the origins and evolution of the French aristocracy, a controversial topic at the time. - Summary by MrCrocodile

With encouragement from Nikita’s scheming mother, the pair begin to look for a way to be together. What follows is a grim tale of jealousy and murder, as one bad deed leads to another and the consequences become increasingly difficult to escape. The Power of Darkness is one of Leo Tolstoy’s best-known plays, and a bleak portrayal of life and morality among the Russian peasantry. 22971.d: In his thirty-fifth year, [John Milton] entered into the marriage state, at Whitsuntide, 1643, with Mary, the daughter of Richard Powell, of Forest-Hill. Whatever was the reason, 'tis certain, that after he had enjoyed her company at London for about a month, she was invited by her friends to spend the rest of the summer in the country: to which he consented, on condition that she returned at Michaelmas. Yet he saw her not at the time appointed, and after receiving several of his letters without sending him any answer, she did at length positively refuse to come, dismissing his messenger with contempt. As all his attempts to induce his wife to return to his house proved ineffectual, he thought his own reputation and repose demanded that he should declare her to be no longer his wife! It is said that he endeavoured to make his constrained widowhood, for nearly four years, as easy and cheerful as he could. Having taken his firm resolution to repudiate his wife, and never to receive her back again, he thought it proper publicly to attempt a justification of this step, and therefore published, in the year 1644, his work on the "Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce." The grand position ho maintains is, "That indisposition, unfitness, and contrary humours, proceeding from any unchangeable cause in nature, hindering, and always likely to hinder, the main ends and benefits of conjugal society, that is to say, peace and delight, are greater reasons of divorce than adultery, or natural frigidity, provided there be a mutual consent for separation." On this book appearing, the clergy in general declaimed against it, charging its author with atheism, heresy, lewdness, &c. &c. They daily instigated the Parliament, but in vain, to pass their censure of condemnation upon it; This, and the opposition to it by some other ministers, led him to publish his Tetrachordon, which also was dedicated to the Parliament. He published yet another piece on this subject, entitled, "The Judgments of the famous Reformer, Martin Bucer, touching Divorce, extracted out of the second book of the kingdom of Christ, dedicated to king Edward the Sixth." Bucer exactly agreed with Milton on this subject, though the latter had not seen it till after the publication of his first volume concerning it. - Summary by Joseph Ivimey

The following stories are written by: Cleveland Moffett, Edgar Allan Poe, Nathanial Hawthorne, Wilkie Collins, Villiers de l'Isle Adam, Florence Marryat, William Archer, Fitz-James O' Brien, and an anonymous writer. - Summary by Patty Harden
